951 male and 1329 female participants across the 2280 participants.

Participants were recruited into four study groups: no type 1 or type 2 diabetes; pre-type 2 diabetes or type 2 diabetes controlled by lifestyle adjustments; type 2 diabetes controlled by oral or non-insulin injectable medications; and insulin-controlled type 2 diabetes.
776 participants with no diabetes, 560 lifestyle-controlled, 686 controlled by oral or non-insulin injectable medication and 258 insulin-controlled.
Eligibility required an age of 40 years or older, with a protocol maximum of 85 years.
Mean age 60.8 ± 11.3 years across the 2280 participants.

The release includes a recommended split into training (1576 participants), validation (352) and test (352) sets, assigned per participant in participants.tsv. Because sex, race and ethnicity are not released with the public version, the project team prepared splits in 70%/15%/15% proportions in which the validation and test sets are balanced as well as possible for sex, race/ethnicity and diabetes status (no diabetes, prediabetes/lifestyle controlled, oral medication controlled, and insulin controlled). Mean age is 61.1 ± 11.3 years in the training set, 60.3 ± 10.8 in validation and 60.5 ± 11.4 in test. The recommended split is new in version 3.0.0 and is intended to reduce disparities in models developed using this dataset.
In survey data, skipped questions or incomplete responses are expected.

In wearable data, improper use and technical failure such as battery failure or system malfunction are expected. The Garmin Vivosmart 5 had to be charged every 2-3 days, so there are gaps in activity data collection.
In imaging data, patient uncooperation, noise that may obscure the images, technical failure such as system malfunction, and data transfer failures are expected.

Undilated handheld fundus photography with the Optomed Aurora is challenging because the pupil is not dilated and the camera is handheld, so image quality varies from patient to patient and within the same patient.

FLIO acquisition takes longer than a standard Spectralis OCT and exposes participants to uncomfortable levels of light, so it is performed last in the visit and participants may not be at their best possible compliance; the device cannot tolerate more than one centimeter of movement during acquisition.
Devices operated manually rather than automatically (for example the Heidelberg Spectralis) can raise quality issues that led to skipping a modality and missing data.
Participants are volunteers, so there is selection bias known as volunteer bias which may limit the generalizability of the results among those who are not represented in the study population.

While the cross-sectional database ultimately aims to achieve balance across race/ethnicity, biological sex, and diabetes presence and severity, the pilot phase is not balanced across these parameters, and enrollment is ongoing so periodic releases may not have achieved balanced distribution across groups. The cohort does not include other races/ethnicities such as Pacific Islanders and Native Americans.

Triple-balanced recruitment targets for race/ethnicity, diabetes severity and biological sex, with under- and oversampling of groups as recruitment progresses; three geographically distinct recording sites recruiting individuals from all demographic backgrounds; recommended training/validation/test splits balanced for sex, race/ethnicity and diabetes status.

Recruitment is predominantly urban and hospital-based, drawn from patients with an encounter in each site's health system, which may not fully capture all possible cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds.

Uniform data collection protocols were implemented for all subjects irrespective of their race/ethnicity, biological sex, or diabetes severity, across all study sites, and the selection of study sites was intended to ensure varied representation and minimize the potential for sampling bias.

Requiring that eligible participants speak, read and understand English may have created challenges in recruiting Hispanic and/or Asian persons; non-English-speaking participants were not initially enrolled because translating all study materials was not feasible.

The study cohort may not provide a comprehensive representation of the population: recruitment is predominantly urban and hospital-based and the cohort does not include races/ethnicities such as Pacific Islanders and Native Americans.
Models derived from the dataset may not generalize to populations, settings or cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds that the three recruiting health systems do not reach.
Not all modalities are available for all participants, because some participants declined some study elements and some device data were lost or unretrievable.

The public release excludes sensitive personal health data: 5-digit zip code, sex, race, ethnicity, genetic sequencing data, past health records, medications, and traffic and accident reports are held under controlled access, and the raw, pre-standardization data are not shared.

The design is cross-sectional with currently one visit per participant; only about 10% of the cohort is planned to return for a follow-up visit in year 4 of the project, so longitudinal trajectories cannot be observed within this release.

Multiple imaging devices were deliberately used for one measure to represent the broad range of equipment in clinical settings, so device make, model and scan protocol differ across participants and must be accounted for; device and modality information is documented to support repeatability.

The healthsheet answers "No" to whether the dataset contains data that, if viewed directly, might be offensive, insulting, threatening, or might otherwise pose any safety risk such as psychological safety and anxiety.
The dataset does not contain data that might be considered confidential, and no personally identifiable information is included in the dataset.

The public dataset does not contain data considered sensitive: it carries no protected health information, and information related to the sex and race/ethnicity of participants and to medications used has been removed.

Reliance agreements were in place with the IRBs of the University of Alabama at Birmingham and the University of California, San Diego.
University of Washington Institutional Review Board (Human Subjects Division, IRB Reliance Team, hsdrely@uw.edu, 4333 Brooklyn Ave NE Box 359470, Seattle, WA 98195-9470)

Human subject review status recorded as submitted and approved; the study is recorded as not FDA-regulated for either drug or device and as having no data monitoring committee; the release carries a confidentiality level of HL7:2N (normal).

Eligibility is limited to adults aged 40 years and older (protocol maximum 85 years) who are able to provide consent and to read and speak English; pregnancy, gestational diabetes and type 1 diabetes are exclusion criteria.

Minors are excluded by the minimum age of 40 years; pregnancy and gestational diabetes are exclusion criteria; the IRB protocol records that the research is not likely to have subjects who become prisoners while participating and that it will not recruit or obtain data from individuals known to be prisoners.

Stipend for the study visit, paid through the grant funding; reasonable parking, public transit or rideshare costs related to the study visit are also covered, and transportation assistance through rideshare services was offered to participants who endorsed barriers to transporting themselves to study visits.

Per the IRB protocol the stipend is provided once the final data are received and the study devices are returned, typically at least two weeks after the study visit, and is not prorated; transport costs above $25 may not be reimbursed.

Directly observable measurements taken during the study visit and the at-home monitoring period, including laboratory tests, vitals, physical measurements, vision and cognitive testing, electrocardiography, retinal imaging, continuous glucose monitoring, wearable activity monitoring and home environmental sensing.

Participant-reported data, principally the pre-visit and in-visit questionnaires completed in REDCap. Verification of data entry was performed when possible, for example by cross- referencing entered medications with medications that were physically brought in or photographed by each study participant.

REDCap was used to collect patient-reported questionnaire data and clinical data from the visit, including the medications assessment, vitals, visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, monofilament test results and complete blood count results; the exact forms used for data collection in REDCap are published with the documentation.

Standardized questionnaires administered through REDCap, including a screening questionnaire, demographic information, the Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale (CES-D-10), Problem Areas in Diabetes (PAID-5), a diabetes self-care score, a dietary assessment, an ophthalmic/visual impairment and eye care survey, smoking, alcohol, vaping and marijuana use history (marijuana not assessed in Alabama), a general health history, PhenX social determinants of health surveys, and a current medications log with RxNorm codes.
12-lead electrocardiography with the Philips PageWriter TC30 Cardiograph, performed with the participant reclining or supine and the chair position recorded.

Blood pressure and heart rate measured twice with automatic oscillometric devices: OMRON HEM 907XL, Medline MDS4001 Automatic Digital Blood Pressure Monitor, or Welch Allyn 6000 series vital signs monitor with a FlexiPort reusable cuff.
10 g monofilament testing of touch perception at three locations on each foot for peripheral neuropathy, with results recorded on an iPad, laptop or paper questionnaire and entered into REDCap.
Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) administered electronically on an iPad using the MoCA Duo application, capturing the total score, section subscores, Memory Index Score and task completion times.

Visual acuity measured with the M&S Technologies Electronic Visual Acuity (EVA) tester at 4 meters under photopic conditions and under mesopic conditions using a 2.0 neutral density filter, each eye separately and best corrected.
Letter contrast sensitivity measured with the MARS Letter Contrast Sensitivity test (Perceptrix) monocularly under photopic and mesopic (neutral density occluder) conditions.
Autorefraction with the Topcon KR 800 auto keratometer/refractor, and lensometry with the NIDEK LM-600P, Topcon CL-200 or Topcon CL-300 lensometers.
Undilated handheld color fundus photography with the Optomed Aurora IQ, a non-mydriatic handheld camera with a 50 degree field of view and 5 Mpix sensor.

Dilated widefield TrueColor confocal fundus imaging with the iCare EIDON, in fully automated mode, capturing single-field central infrared and fundus autofluorescence images and a smart horizontal mosaic.
Optical coherence tomography and OCT angiography with the Heidelberg Spectralis HRA+OCT using the ONH-RC, PPole-H and macular OCTA protocols.
Fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscopy with the Heidelberg FLIO, macula-centered, acquired last in the visit.
Swept-source OCT and OCTA with the Topcon DRI OCT Triton, using 12.0 x 12.0 mm and 6.0 x 6.0 mm OCTA and 12.0 x 9.0 x 6.0 mm 3D horizontal and radial scan modes.
OCT, OCTA and color fundus photography with the Topcon Maestro2 3D OCT-1 robotic system, using 12.0 x 9.0 mm widefield, 6.0 x 6.0 mm 3D macula and 6.0 x 6.0 mm OCTA (50 kHz) protocols.
OCT and OCTA with the Zeiss Cirrus 5000 Angioplex, using 512 x 512 and 200 x 200 macula and optic nerve head scans and macular OCTA.

Dexcom G6 real-time integrated continuous glucose monitoring system, worn continuously for 10 days after the visit, capturing readings every five minutes; participants were masked to the results during the monitoring period.

Garmin Vivosmart 5 fitness activity tracker, worn for 10 consecutive days on the participant's chosen wrist, with the wrist worn and the dominant hand recorded on a returned data sheet; sampling frequency 5 seconds.

LeeLab Anura, an environmental sensor unit custom designed for the AI-READI project at the Karalis Johnson Retina Center, University of Washington, placed in a frequently used area of the participant's home for 10 days; the placement location was recorded on return.

Non-fasting blood and urine collection during the visit, with complete blood counts run by Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments-certified laboratories local to each data collection site and all other assays performed by the University of Washington Nutrition and Obesity Research Center testing facility on stored frozen samples.
Clinical research coordinators and research staff

Research personnel at the three data sites who recruited, enrolled and collected data underwent training by the data manager at the University of Alabama at Birmingham and worked from a detailed Manual of Procedures; a certification process was required of all coordinators, including mandatory institutional compliance training for human subject research and successful administration of all protocol elements to at least three volunteer practice subjects.
Data managers at each site oversaw the data collection process and were responsible for the quality control of all data before uploading to FAIRhub.
Once data were sent from each of the study sites to the central project team, additional processing steps were conducted in preparation for dissemination.

Effort of the team members involved in data collection was supported by NIH award OT2OD032644 based on the percentage of effort contributed, with salaries aligned to the funding guidelines at each site.

Version 3.0.0 covers data collected from July 19, 2023 to May 1, 2025, that is through the end of the second full year of the study. The overall project timeline spans four years, one year for protocol development and training and years 2-4 for subject recruitment and data collection; the study start date is recorded as 2023-07-19 (actual) with an anticipated completion date of 2027-01-01, and the overall status is "Enrolling by invitation".
The BMJ Open protocol publication states that enrollment began on 18 July 2023 and will continue until 30 November 2026, one day earlier than the start date recorded in the dataset metadata.

The data was collected directly from participants across the three recruiting sites; this was active data collection rather than passive collection or secondary use of existing data. Recruitment pools were identified by screening electronic health records for diabetes and prediabetes ICD-10 codes among patients with an encounter in the sites' health systems.

Non-probability sampling. A contact pool was identified for each recruitment wave by screening electronic health records at each site using ICD-10 codes (R73.09 for pre-diabetes and E11.X for T2DM) and demographic data; invitations were mailed and emailed with personalized links into an online REDCap recruitment interface. Recruitment proceeded in waves whose composition and size were influenced by the observed participation characteristics of race/ethnicity, gender, severity of T2DM and site, with under- and oversampling of groups as needed.
All patients aged 40 years or older who had a medical encounter within each health system site (University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of California San Diego, University of Washington).

Rather than targeting the demographic distribution of the US population, the study is triple-balanced by recruiting four race/ethnic groups (Asian, black, white, Hispanic), four categories of T2DM severity and biological males and females in equal proportions, because building balanced datasets is critical for the development of unbiased machine learning models.

The healthsheet states that the dataset contains all possible instances, that is data from all participants enrolled by the data cut-off, and answers "N/A" to the question about sampling strategy for a sample of a larger set; the study itself is recorded as a non-probability sample of the health-system population described above.
Electronic health records at the three recruiting sites, screened for ICD-10 diabetes and prediabetes diagnosis codes and demographic data to identify recruitment pools.
Used for recruitment screening only; not released as part of the dataset.

Device-native exports written to local storage before standardization: ECG in .xml, MoCA Duo application output in .csv, retinal imaging in DICOM or in vendor formats (.fda for Topcon Maestro2 and Triton, .sdt for FLIO) later converted to DICOM, Garmin fitness tracker data in .FIT later converted to the Open mHealth standard, and Dexcom CGM and environmental sensor data in .csv.

The raw data is saved and expected to be preserved by the AI-READI project at least for the duration of the project, but is not anticipated to be shared outside the project team at present because it has not been mapped to standardized terminologies and may accidentally include personal health information or personally identifiable information, for example in free text fields; there is a possibility that raw data may be included in future releases of the controlled access dataset.

Quality control measures were applied at the time of data entry and acquisition: clinical data outside expected minimum/maximum ranges were flagged in REDCap and surfaced in reports viewed by clinical research coordinators and data managers, who examined participant records to determine whether an error was likely. Data were checked, and edited where errors were detected, for credibility against prespecified reasonable ranges, incorrect flow through prescribed skip patterns, missing data that could be filled directly from other portions of an individual's record, and the omission or duplication of records. Editing was done only under the guidance and approval of the site principal investigator; where there was no logical or appropriate way to correct a value, the site PI decided whether it should be removed.

After data were sent from the study sites to the central project team, all data were mapped to standardized terminologies where possible, including the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model for clinical data and DICOM for medical imaging; proprietary device exports were transformed into standard model formats before upload to FAIRhub, with Topcon .fda and FLIO .sdt files converted to DICOM and Garmin .FIT files converted to the Open mHealth standard. Processing for this release combined automated and custom steps, in contrast with the custom/ad hoc processing of version 1.0.0.

No instances were excluded at the time of preprocessing; exclusions arise only from the study eligibility criteria (age 40 or older, able to consent, able to read and speak English, not pregnant, no gestational diabetes, no type 1 diabetes).

Electrocardiogram data collected by a 12 lead protocol (the current standard), Holter monitor, or smartwatch; the terms ECG and EKG are often used interchangeably. Data in this release were collected with the Philips PageWriter TC30 (ecg_12lead/philips_tc30). A manifest.tsv metadata file based on the Clinical Dataset Structure is included.
WaveForm DataBase (WFDB); directory layout per Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS) v0.1.1

Clinical data collected through REDCap, including blood and urine lab values and survey data, formatted to the OMOP Common Data Model; each CSV file in this directory is a one-to-one mapping to the OMOP CDM tables. The data comprise health-related measurements and assessments including lab tests, MoCA cognitive testing, monofilament testing, physical and vision assessments, and survey questionnaire results. A dqd_omop.json file supports OMOP CDM data quality analysis with the OMOP CDM Data Quality Dashboard.
Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model

Data collected through an environmental sensor device custom built for the AI-READI project, the LeeLab Anura (environmental_sensor/leelab_anura), placed in a frequently used area of each participant's home for 10 days. The sensor recorded particulate matter counts (PM 1.0, 2.5, 4 and 10), temperature, relative humidity, volatile organic compounds, nitrogen oxides (NO and NO2) and 11 multi-spectral light intensity measurements.
ASCII File Format Guidelines for Earth Science Data (NASA recommended practices for formatting and describing ASCII encoded data files)

Data collected through fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscopy (FLIO), an imaging modality for in vivo measurement of lifetimes of endogenous retinal fluorophores, acquired on the Heidelberg FLIO (flio/heidelberg_flio). The scan records images at two wavelength channels, short (498-560 nm) and long (560-720 nm), provided as two separate DICOM files for each eye.
Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM)

Data collected using optical coherence tomography (OCT), a non-invasive diagnostic technique that renders an in vivo cross-sectional view of the retina using interferometry. The structural_oct modality holds data from four devices: heidelberg_spectralis, topcon_maestro2, topcon_triton and zeiss_cirrus.
Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM)

Data collected using optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), a non-invasive imaging technique that generates volumetric angiography images by mapping red blood cell movement over time from sequential OCT scans, without dye injection. Three modalities are included - enface (2D views derived from 3D volume scans), flow_cube (3D blood flow information) and segmentation (heightmaps with associated layer information) - each from heidelberg_spectralis, topcon_maestro2, topcon_triton and zeiss_cirrus.
Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM)

Retinal photography data: two-dimensional images of the posterior segment of the eye, also referred to as fundus photography, used to document the optic nerve, macula, retinal vasculature and central and peripheral retina. Modalities are cfp (color fundus photography, from icare_eidon, optomed_aurora, topcon_maestro2 and topcon_triton), faf (fundus autofluorescence, from icare_eidon) and ir (near-infrared reflectance, from heidelberg_spectralis, icare_eidon, topcon_maestro2 and zeiss_cirrus).

Data collected through a wearable fitness tracker, the Garmin Vivosmart 5 (garmin_vivosmart5), worn for 10 consecutive days. Modalities are heart_rate, oxygen_saturation, physical_activity, physical_activity_calorie, respiratory_rate, sleep and stress.

Informed consent to participate was required before participation in any part of the protocol, including questionnaires. Potential participants were given the option to read all consent documentation electronically (e-consent) before their visit and to give consent with an electronic signature in REDCap without verbal communication with a clinical research coordinator, and could decide at that point not to participate or to request additional information; consent could otherwise be given in person at the start of the visit. Participants received an email with a unique code to access their e-consent. The approved consent form for the principal project site, the University of Washington, is published with the version 3.0.0 documentation; the other clinical sites had IRB reliance and used the same consent form with minor institution-specific language.
Written informed consent, obtained either electronically (e-consent with electronic signature in REDCap) or in person at the start of the visit.
Signed consent forms; the approved University of Washington consent form is included with the version 3.0.0 documentation.

FAIRhub records the dataset consent type as "ConsentSpecifiedNotElsewhereCategorised": the public version of the dataset can only be used for type 2 diabetes related research, while a private version will allow for more generic use.

Each individual was aware of the data collection, as this was not passive data collection or secondary use of existing data but active data collection directly from participants. Individuals in each recruitment pool were mailed a hardcopy invitation letter and sent an invitation email, both personalized, directing them into an online REDCap recruitment interface where they could read an overview of the research program, expectations for participation and answers to frequently asked questions, download the informed consent document, request a call back from study staff, complete a screening survey and enroll.

Participants were permitted to withdraw consent at any time and cease study participation. However, any data that had been shared or used up to that point would stay in the dataset. This is clearly communicated in the consent document.
University of Washington Institutional Review Board

The study was approved under protocol STUDY00016228, with initial IRB approval received on December 20, 2022 and an annual renewal application required within 90 days of expiration; reliance agreements were in place with the IRBs of the University of Alabama at Birmingham and the University of California, San Diego. The initial approval letter is published with the version 3.0.0 documentation. The contact is the IRB Reliance Team, hsdrely@uw.edu, Human Subjects Division, 4333 Brooklyn Ave NE Box 359470, Seattle, WA 98195-9470.

The RO-Crate records ethical review of the release by Camille Nebeker, Debra Mathews, Kadija Ferryman and Nicholas Evans. Ethical, legal and social implications are considered at every stage of the project cycle, with guidance from bioethicists.

Accessing the dataset requires logging in through a verified ID system, agreeing to use the data only for type 2 diabetes related research, and agreeing to the license terms, which set certain restrictions and obligations for data usage. FAIRhub records the access type as "PublicDownloadSelfAttestationRequired" and publishes the conditions of access at https://fairhub.io/datasets/3/access.

The data manager at each data site is responsible for the quality control of all data before uploading to FAIRhub; the AI-READI team supports and maintains the dataset, which is hosted on FAIRhub through Microsoft Azure. The RO-Crate names the AI-READI Consortium as the data governance committee.

The BMJ Open protocol publication states that the requirements for the controlled access dataset were being developed by a Data Access Committee, and that procedures for reviewing and prioritizing written requests for biorepository samples would be developed before the biorepository is complete.

The dataset is released under a custom license, the AI-READI Data License Agreement version 2.0 (Washington University in St. Louis as Licensor; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17555036), tailored to enable reuse of the AI-READI dataset and other clinical datasets for commercial or research purposes while imposing strong requirements around data usage, security and secondary sharing to protect study participants, especially when data is reused for AI and ML applications. It grants a non-exclusive, non-transferable license to download, reproduce and use the data and to create derivative works for research, commercial and non-commercial purposes. Derivative and synthetic data derived from the data are themselves treated as data subject to the same restrictions. The license requires acknowledgement of the Licensor, the source and any funder in papers reporting use of the data, and compliance with NIH Genomic Data Sharing Policy security standards. It terminates automatically upon any breach by the licensee or an authorized user, after which all copies must be deleted and all use must cease. The data are provided "as is", without warranty of any kind.

Title to the data, and all industrial and intellectual property rights therein, remain solely and exclusively with the Licensor and its suppliers, and any rights not expressly granted in the license are reserved. Licensees are permitted to make, reproduce and distribute models, algorithms and programs developed, trained or adapted using the data provided those models do not themselves contain the data or any modified version of it, and provided that before dissemination the licensee undertakes all reasonable efforts to minimize the likelihood that data can be memorized, derived, reconstructed or reconstituted through their use or construction. The release carries the copyright notice "Copyright © 2026 AI-READI". The healthsheet states that questions about third-party IP-based restrictions are answered by reference to the license.

Licensees must comply with all data security and privacy standards established by the U.S. National Institutes of Health under its Genomic Data Sharing (GDS) Policy, currently the NIH Security Best Practices for Controlled-Access Data Subject to the NIH GDS Policy, and with all applicable laws, regulations and restrictions relating to the distribution and use of the data and of models. values.text: Flagship Dataset of Type 2 Diabetes from the AI-READI Project

Version 3.0.0 of the Flagship Dataset of Type 2 Diabetes from the AI-READI project: a multimodal, AI-ready dataset assembled from 2,280 adults with and without type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and harmonized across three United States data collection sites (the University of Alabama at Birmingham, the University of California San Diego, and the University of Washington). Data were collected between 19 July 2023 and 1 May 2025 through a single in-person study visit of roughly three to four hours followed by a ten-day at-home monitoring period in which participants wore a continuous glucose monitor and a fitness tracker and placed an environmental sensor in their home. The release covers survey and social-determinants-of-health responses, blood and urine laboratory results, physical and vision assessments, monofilament and cognitive testing, 12-lead electrocardiography, retinal photography, optical coherence tomography (OCT), OCT angiography (OCTA), fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscopy (FLIO), continuous glucose monitoring, wearable activity monitoring, and indoor environmental sensing. It comprises 356,343 files totaling approximately 3.82 TB, organized following the Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS) v0.1.1 as one directory per data type, then modality, then device, then participant. The dataset is hypothesis-agnostic and carries no labels or targets; a recommended train/validation/test assignment is supplied in participants.tsv. This record describes the publicly downloadable FAIRhub release identified by DOI 10.60775/fairhub.3; banked biospecimens held at the University of Alabama at Birmingham and the companion controlled-access release are not part of it.
AI-READI Consortium. (2025). Flagship Dataset of Type 2 Diabetes from the AI-READI Project (3.0.0) [Data set]. FAIRhub. https://doi.org/10.60775/fairhub.3

The dataset as a whole is organized following the Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS) v0.1.1 and is additionally packaged as an RO-Crate conforming to the RO-Crate 1.2 draft profile. Within it, retinal photography, OCT, OCTA and FLIO files follow the Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) standard; clinical data files follow the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model; electrocardiogram files follow the WaveForm DataBase (WFDB) standard; wearable activity and continuous glucose monitoring files follow Open mHealth; and environmental sensor files follow the NASA ASCII File Format Guidelines for Earth Science Data.

Both the FAIRhub dataset pages and the AI-READI documentation site carry the notice "This repository is under review for potential modification in compliance with Administration directives." At the point the FAIRhub API record was captured, version 3.0.0 reported a view count of 24,636 and a citation count of 0.

This record describes the publicly downloadable FAIRhub release of version 3.0.0 (DOI 10.60775/fairhub.3). Sources disagree on the expansion of the acronym: the FAIRhub study description and NIH RePORTER give "Artificial Intelligence Ready and Exploratory Atlas for Diabetes Insights", while the BMJ Open protocol and the Nature Metabolism comment give "Artificial Intelligence Ready and Equitable Atlas for Diabetes Insights"; the higher-ranked FAIRhub metadata is followed here. Sources also disagree on the lead institution: the FAIRhub structured metadata names Washington University in St. Louis as managing organization and lead sponsor and the license names it as Licensor, while the RO-Crate places the principal investigator in the Department of Ophthalmology at the University of Washington and NIH RePORTER records the awardee organization as the University of Washington; the two disagreeing tier-1 sources share the same rank, so both are recorded. Publisher is likewise disputed between the two tier-1 sources: the FAIRhub structured metadata gives "FAIRhub" and the RO-Crate gives "AI-READI Consortium"; the FAIRhub value is recorded in `publisher` and the RO-Crate value noted here. Enrollment target is given as 4,000 participants by the FAIRhub study description, the NIH RePORTER abstract and both publications, but as 4,600 by the University of Washington IRB protocol.

Organizational creator of record for the dataset, registered in the DataCite creator block with nameType Organizational. The consortium comprises the members of the AI-READI project across its participating institutions.
Department of Ophthalmology, University of Washington

Two affiliations are recorded because two equally ranked tier-1 sources disagree: the FAIRhub structured metadata gives Aaron Lee's responsible-party and central contact affiliation as Washington University in St. Louis (ROR 01yc7t268), while the RO-Crate names him as principal investigator in the Department of Ophthalmology at the University of Washington. The email is the study central contact address recorded against his FAIRhub central-contact entry.

The affiliation list is the collaborator and location roster recorded in the FAIRhub study description; the consortium itself carries no registry identifier in the declared sources, so no id is asserted for it.
"Bridge2AI: Salutogenesis Data Generation Project", awarded through the NIH Common Fund Bridge2AI program; the RO-Crate cites the award as 1OT2OD032644.

The FAIRhub award record links OT2OD032644 to NIH RePORTER project-details/10885481, while the RO-Crate acknowledgement and the declared NIH RePORTER source link the same core project number to application 10471118 (project number 1OT2OD032644-01). The Nature Metabolism comment writes the second grant as "P30 DK035816"; the BMJ Open protocol writes it without the space, which is the form used here. P30DK035816 and UL1TR003096 are named only in the BMJ Open protocol acknowledgement.
Named alongside the NIH grants in the funding statement of the BMJ Open protocol publication.

To create and publicly share a flagship, ethically sourced, AI-ready multimodal dataset on type 2 diabetes mellitus so that future artificial intelligence/machine-learning research can produce insights into the disease, including salutogenic pathways back to health.

To serve as a blueprint for future data-generation projects by establishing standards, best practices and guidelines for the collection, preparation and sharing of AI-ready clinical research datasets, including new standards such as the Clinical Dataset Structure.

To assemble a cohort balanced across self-reported race/ethnicity, biological sex and diabetes disease stage, so that models trained on the data are not skewed by the demographic imbalances of earlier type 2 diabetes cohorts. The study's anticipated enrollment is 4,000 participants across the three sites.

The absence of well-designed, high-quality, large and inclusive multimodal datasets that are AI-ready for training models on complex, multi-organ diseases such as type 2 diabetes mellitus; the project identifies this lack of AI-ready data as the key barrier to AI-based understanding of the disease.

Under-representation of racialized groups in type 2 diabetes research: a meta-epidemiological review of type 2 diabetes studies published from 2000 to 2020 found that samples lacked racial and ethnic diversity, and the deleterious consequences of the disease are exacerbated in the populations that bear the higher burden.

The limited utility of existing data sources such as insurance claims and electronic health records for downstream AI/ML analyses, which the project addresses by designing a purpose-built acquisition protocol spanning survey, physical, clinical, imaging and wearable-device domains.

Downstream pseudotime manifold analysis: an approach used to predict disease trajectories by learning from complex, multimodal data collected from participants spanning the range of disease severity, from normal to insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes mellitus.
Reconstruction of a temporal atlas of type 2 diabetes development and reversal towards health (salutogenesis), from a foundational dataset that is agnostic to existing classification criteria.
artificial intelligence and machine learning research
Multimodal model development for type 2 diabetes mellitus; prediction of disease trajectories; study of salutogenesis.
Data are stored and shared as "AI-ready" so that AI/ML research can begin without further reformatting or preprocessing.

Access to the public release is conditioned on agreeing to use the data only for type 2 diabetes related research; the project documentation states that a private version will allow for more generic use.
Making clinical treatment decisions based on the data.
The data are intended solely as a research resource.

Using or attempting to use the data, alone or with other information, to compromise the confidentiality or privacy of a data subject, to identify or contact any data subject or group of data subjects, to extract or extrapolate identifying information, to establish a data subject's membership in a particular group, or otherwise to cause harm or injury to a data subject.
Protection of study participants against re-identification and harm.

Sharing or distributing the data with any third-party model vendor or developer for training or development purposes, including model weight modification and other adjustments to a model's logic or operation, even where that vendor holds a HIPAA-approved Business Associate Agreement with the licensee's institution. Short-term interaction such as prompting or querying a third-party model covered by such an agreement is permitted for analysis.
Prevention of memorization or reconstruction of the data by externally controlled models.

Transferring, licensing, sublicensing, selling, assigning, displaying or otherwise conveying any portion of the data or any derivative work to any third party other than another licensee bound by an identical agreement with the licensor.
Secondary sharing controls in the license, to keep all recipients bound by the same obligations.

Reproducing data in papers, articles, presentations, analyses, reports or publications beyond small representative samples in up to five images or figures per paper; larger amounts may not be published, posted or made available through supplemental files, zip archives, code packages or other means, notwithstanding journal or conference requirements.
Publication controls in the license; publishers and conference organizers may seek a separate license from the licensor.

Storing the data anywhere other than servers and devices maintained by and located within the licensee's institution or employer, or on cloud or remote storage and backup services covered by a HIPAA-approved Business Associate Agreement with that institution or employer.
Data security requirements in the license.
Removing, obscuring, altering or masking the static watermarking that may be applied to the data to identify the licensee.
Watermarking is a security control identifying the licensee.

The dataset creators do not currently anticipate uses of the dataset that could result in unfair treatment of individuals or groups or other undesirable harms; however, they acknowledge a theoretical risk of future re-identification.

Because sex, race and ethnicity are withheld from the public release, users of that release cannot directly stratify or audit model performance across those groups. The project mitigates this by supplying a recommended training/validation/testing split whose validation and test sets are balanced as well as possible for sex, race/ethnicity and diabetes status, with the stated aim of reducing disparities in models developed from the dataset.
No labels or targets are provided. No specific labeling was performed, because the dataset is hypothesis-agnostic and aimed at facilitating multiple potential downstream AI/ML applications.
Not all modalities are available for all participants.

Some participants elected not to take part in some study elements; in a few cases the data collection device had no stored results or was returned too late for the results to be retrieved (battery died, data lost); and in a few cases a data collision at some point in the process led to lost data.

Each instance consists of all of the data available for one individual participating in the study, spanning tabular, imaging and physiological signal/waveform data. No unstructured free-text data are included.

All instances belong to the same prospective data generation project (AI-READI). There is currently one study visit per participant, so instances are not linked across visits. Files belonging to one participant are grouped by a participant folder named after the participant's study ID number within each device directory.

Self-reported race and ethnicity, recorded at screening in four groups (Hispanic, Asian, Black, White). Individual race and ethnicity values are withheld from the public release and held under controlled access; only the aggregate breakdown is published in the dataset README.
Across the 2,280 participants: 380 Hispanic, 545 Asian, 519 Black, 836 White.
Biological sex, self-reported at screening. Individual values are withheld from the public release and held under controlled access; only the aggregate breakdown is published in the dataset README.

Diabetes status group, one of the four study arms: no Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes; pre-Type 2 diabetes or Type 2 diabetes controlled by lifestyle adjustment; Type 2 diabetes controlled by oral or non-insulin injectable medication; Type 2 diabetes controlled by insulin.
Across the 2,280 participants: 776 with no diabetes, 560 pre-diabetes or lifestyle-controlled, 686 controlled by oral or non-insulin injectable medication, 258 insulin-controlled.
Age at study visit; eligibility was restricted to adults aged 40 years and older, with the study description recording a maximum age of 85 years.
Mean age across the 2,280 participants is 60.8 years (standard deviation 11.3).

The FAIRhub healthsheet answers "No" to the question of whether the dataset itself identifies demographic sub-populations; the distributions recorded here are the aggregate summary tables published in the dataset README, not per-instance labels in the public release.

Training partition recommended by the project team, covering 1,576 participants. Composition reported in the dataset README: 204 Hispanic, 369 Asian, 343 Black and 660 White; 599 male and 977 female; 600 with no diabetes, 384 pre-diabetes or lifestyle-controlled, 487 controlled by oral or non-insulin injectable medication and 105 insulin-controlled; mean age 61.1 years (standard deviation 11.3).

Validation partition recommended by the project team, covering 352 participants. Composition reported in the dataset README: 88 each of Hispanic, Asian, Black and White; 176 male and 176 female; 88 with no diabetes, 88 pre-diabetes or lifestyle-controlled, 109 controlled by oral or non-insulin injectable medication and 67 insulin-controlled; mean age 60.3 years (standard deviation 10.8).

Test partition recommended by the project team, covering 352 participants. Composition reported in the dataset README: 88 each of Hispanic, Asian, Black and White; 176 male and 176 female; 88 with no diabetes, 88 pre-diabetes or lifestyle-controlled, 90 controlled by oral or non-insulin injectable medication and 86 insulin-controlled; mean age 60.5 years (standard deviation 11.4).

A 70%/15%/15% training/validation/testing assignment is supplied per participant in the participants.tsv file included with the dataset. Because sex, race and ethnicity are not released with the public version, the project team constructed the assignment so that the validation and test sets are balanced as well as possible for sex, race/ethnicity and diabetes status; the split was introduced with version 3.0.0 and also balances for age and study group.

The split is a recommendation rather than a constraint; no tasks or labels accompany it, and the project team states it has no formal guidelines for researchers who define new tasks or create new labels.

Electrocardiogram data collected using the 12-lead protocol, organized as ecg_12lead/philips_tc30/<participant>. Includes a manifest.tsv metadata file built to the Clinical Dataset Structure specification.
WaveForm DataBase (WFDB); directory layout per Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS) v0.1.1

Clinical data collected through REDCap, including blood and urine laboratory values, MoCA cognitive testing, monofilament testing, physical and vision assessments and survey questionnaire results. Each CSV file is a one-to-one mapping to an OMOP Common Data Model table. A dqd_omop.json file supports analysis with the OMOP CDM Data Quality Dashboard.
Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model; directory named per Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS) v0.1.1

Indoor environmental sensor readings from the LeeLab Anura, a sensor unit custom built for the AI-READI project and placed in each participant's home for ten days. Organized as environmental_sensor/leelab_anura/<participant>.
NASA ASCII File Format Guidelines for Earth Science Data; directory layout per Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS) v0.1.1

Fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscopy data, an imaging modality for in vivo measurement of the lifetimes of endogenous retinal fluorophores, acquired on the Heidelberg FLIO device (flio/heidelberg_flio). Two wavelength channels are provided per eye in separate DICOM files, short (498-560 nm) and long (560-720 nm).
Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM); directory layout per Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS) v0.1.1
Structural optical coherence tomography data acquired on four devices, organized as structural_oct/<device>/<participant>: Heidelberg Spectralis, Topcon Maestro2, Topcon Triton and Zeiss Cirrus.
Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM); directory layout per Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS) v0.1.1

Optical coherence tomography angiography data in three modalities - en face images derived from 3D volume scans, flow cube volumes describing blood flow, and segmentation heightmaps with associated layer information - each acquired on Heidelberg Spectralis, Topcon Maestro2, Topcon Triton and Zeiss Cirrus devices. This is the largest collection by file count in the release.
Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM); directory layout per Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS) v0.1.1

Two-dimensional fundus photography in three modalities: color fundus photographs (cfp) from iCare Eidon, Optomed Aurora, Topcon Maestro2 and Topcon Triton; fundus autofluorescence (faf) from iCare Eidon; and near-infrared reflectance (ir) from Heidelberg Spectralis, iCare Eidon, Topcon Maestro2 and Zeiss Cirrus.
Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM); directory layout per Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS) v0.1.1

Data from the Garmin Vivosmart 5 fitness tracker worn for ten consecutive days, organized into seven modality directories - heart_rate, oxygen_saturation, physical_activity, physical_activity_calorie, respiratory_rate, sleep and stress - each under garmin_vivosmart5/<participant>.
Open mHealth; directory layout per Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS) v0.1.1

Continuous glucose monitoring data from the Dexcom G6, organized as continuous_glucose_monitoring/dexcom_g6/<participant>. Participants wore the device for ten days concurrently with the activity tracker and the home environmental sensor, masked to the readings during the monitoring period.
Open mHealth; directory layout per Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS) v0.1.1

Nine Clinical Dataset Structure metadata and documentation files at the root of the release: CHANGELOG.md, dataset_description.json, dataset_structure_description.json, healthsheet.md, LICENSE.txt, participants.json, participants.tsv, README.md and study_description.json. participants.tsv carries the recommended training/validation/testing assignment; healthsheet.md is the project's own datasheet for the release.

file_count here is this record's own computation, not a figure any source reports: the dataset-level total of 356,343 files minus the 356,334 files accounted for by the nine data-type directory counts reported in the FAIRhub dataset_structure_description (4,515 + 7 + 2,232 + 7,969 + 56,478 + 173,721 + 93,921 + 15,245 + 2,246). The result matches the nine metadata file names listed at the dataset root.
Study participant identifier; each participant folder within a device directory is named after the participant's ID number used in the study.
Recommended assignment to the training, validation or testing partition, supplied per participant in participants.tsv.
Dexcom G6 continuous glucose monitor, sampling every five minutes over a ten-day wear period; the sensor measures glucose in tissue fluid without finger sticks.
Garmin Vivosmart 5 wrist-worn activity monitor; heart rate was additionally read from the electrocardiogram and blood pressure devices during the on-site visit.
Garmin Vivosmart 5 wrist-worn activity monitor; recorded as circadian and diurnal rhythm, with sleep phases.

Montreal Cognitive Assessment administered by research staff on an iPad using the pre-installed MoCA Duo application; six domain-specific index scores, a Memory Index Score and task completion times are recorded alongside the total.

A score of 26 and above is considered normal and anything below 24 is a sign of cognitive impairment; the source notes that a person's level of education, socioeconomic factors, and depression or other mental health conditions may affect the score.

Electronic Visual Acuity tester (M&S Technologies) at four meters under best-corrected conditions, each eye separately, under photopic conditions and under mesopic conditions using a 2.0 neutral density filter.

Mars Letter Contrast Sensitivity chart (Mars Perceptrix) read monocularly under photopic conditions and under mesopic conditions using a neutral density occluder; testing terminated after two consecutive errors or at the end of the chart.
Whole blood test performed by the University of Washington Nutrition and Obesity Research Center laboratory on samples batch-shipped from the collection sites.

The BMJ Open protocol reports units and a reference range for this analyte in a multi-column table whose columns were separated in the bundled text; no unit or range is asserted here because the row alignment could not be read unambiguously.
LeeLab Anura home environmental sensor, over a ten-day placement.
LeeLab Anura home environmental sensor, over a ten-day placement.
LeeLab Anura home environmental sensor; counts reported for the PM1.0, PM2.5, PM4 and PM10 size fractions.
LeeLab Anura home environmental sensor; nitric oxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2).
LeeLab Anura home environmental sensor; eleven multi-spectral light intensity measurements.

Standard 10 g monofilament applied to points on the plantar surface of both feet with shoes and socks removed and the participant's eyes closed; the participant answers yes or no at each site, insensate areas are retested for confirmation, and results are entered into REDCap by clinical research staff.

Directly observable data were measured during the visit or by the take-home devices: laboratory tests on blood and urine, vital signs and physical measurements, vision testing, retinal imaging, 12-lead electrocardiography, monofilament testing, continuous glucose monitoring, wearable activity monitoring and home environmental sensing.

Survey and questionnaire responses were reported by participants through REDCap. Verification of data entry was performed where possible - for example cross-referencing entered medications against medications physically brought in or photographed by the participant.

REDCap electronic data capture, used both for the online recruitment and e-consent interface and for collecting participant-reported questionnaire data and coordinator-entered clinical data (medications assessment, vitals, visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, monofilament results and complete blood count results).

Optomed Aurora IQ handheld non-mydriatic fundus camera (Optomed, Oulu, Finland), 50 degree field of view, 5 Mpix sensor; used undilated in a dark room with the participant reclining. Image quality varies between and within participants because the eye is undilated and the camera is handheld.

iCare EIDON widefield TrueColor confocal fundus imaging system (iCare USA, Raleigh, North Carolina), capturing up to 200 degrees, operated in fully automated mode in a dark room; AI-READI acquires single-field central IR/FAF and a smart horizontal mosaic.

Heidelberg Spectralis HRA+OCT (Heidelberg Engineering, Heidelberg, Germany), combining confocal scanning laser ophthalmoscopy with OCT and angiography; AI-READI protocols are optic nerve head radial circle high resolution, posterior pole macula 61-line high resolution, and 20x20 macular OCTA.

Topcon Maestro2 3D OCT-1 robotic OCT and color fundus camera (Topcon Healthcare, Itabashi-ku, Tokyo, Japan); protocols are 12.0x9.0 mm widefield, 6.0x6.0 mm 3D macula and 6.0x6.0 mm OCTA at a 50 kHz scan rate.

Topcon Triton DRI OCT swept-source system with a 1,050 nm light source and non-mydriatic color fundus camera (Topcon Healthcare); protocols are 12.0x12.0 mm and 6.0x6.0 mm OCTA and 12.0x9.0x6.0 mm 3D horizontal and radial scans.

Zeiss Cirrus 5000 AngioPlex high-definition OCT system (Carl Zeiss Meditec, Jena, Germany); protocols include 512x512 and 200x200 macula and optic nerve head scans, macular OCTA, 8x8 mm single scans and a 14x14 mm automated OCTA montage.

Heidelberg FLIO fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscope (Heidelberg Engineering), macula-centered, exported in .sdt format and converted to DICOM. It is performed last in the visit because it takes longer than a standard Spectralis OCT and exposes participants to uncomfortable light levels.

Philips PageWriter TC30 cardiograph (Philips, Amsterdam, The Netherlands) for 12-lead electrocardiography, performed with the participant reclining or supine and the chair position (0, 30, 60 or 90 degrees relative to supine) recorded; exported as XML.

Dexcom G6 real-time integrated continuous glucose monitoring system (Dexcom, San Diego, California), worn continuously for ten days after the visit; a filament inserted under the skin measures glucose in tissue fluid and the transmitter records readings every five minutes.

Garmin Vivosmart 5 fitness activity tracker (Garmin Ltd, Schaffhausen, Switzerland), worn for ten consecutive days on the participant's chosen wrist at a five-second sampling frequency; participants returned a form recording which wrist was used and their dominant hand.

LeeLab Anura, a home environmental sensor unit custom designed by the Karalis Johnson Retina Center, University of Washington, placed in a frequently used area of the participant's home for ten days; participants recorded where it was placed.

M&S Technologies Electronic Visual Acuity (EVA) tester, administered at four meters on a 12x20 inch touch-screen monitor with the participant's own correction or trial frames; a general occluder is used for photopic testing and a neutral density occluder for mesopic testing.

Mars Letter Contrast Sensitivity test (Mars Perceptrix, Chappaqua, New York), read monocularly at a designed 50 cm viewing distance with near correction, under background luminance of 60 to 120 cd/m2 and illuminance of 189 to 377 lux, in the standardized order photopic right eye, photopic left eye, mesopic right eye, mesopic left eye, all undilated.
Topcon KR 800 auto keratometer/refractor (Topcon Healthcare, Oakland, New Jersey) for autorefraction of each eye, giving spherical and cylindrical components in dioptres with cylindrical axis.
Lensometers, varying by data acquisition site: NIDEK LM-600P auto lensometer, Topcon CL-200 and Topcon CL-300 computerized lensometers.

Automatic oscillometric blood pressure devices, varying by data acquisition site: OMRON HEM 907XL, Medline MDS4001 automatic digital monitor, and Welch Allyn 6000 series vital signs monitor with a Welch Allyn FlexiPort reusable cuff. Systolic, diastolic and heart rate were measured twice, separated by two minutes.
Montreal Cognitive Assessment administered electronically on an iPad using the MoCA Duo application (MoCA Cognition, Quebec, Canada), which captures participant responses interactively.

Standard 10 g monofilament for peripheral neuropathy testing on three locations of each foot, ten times per location, with the participant's eyes closed and shoes and socks removed; results are entered on an iPad, laptop or paper questionnaire and added to REDCap by clinical research staff.

Clinical laboratory testing: Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments-certified laboratories local to each collection site performed complete blood counts on fresh whole blood, and all other assays were performed by the University of Washington Nutrition and Obesity Research Center testing facility on stored frozen samples batch-shipped on dry ice approximately quarterly.

Data were collected directly from participants at the three recruiting sites, not obtained via third parties. Recruitment pools were first identified by screening each site's electronic health records for diabetes and pre-diabetes ICD-10 codes among patients with a recent encounter in that health system, after which individuals were invited by mailed letter and email to enroll through the study's REDCap interface.

The period during which the data in version 3.0.0 were collected, spanning the pilot phase and the first two years of the main study. The overall project timeline spans four years, with one year for protocol development and training and years two to four for recruitment and data collection.

The FAIRhub metadata and healthsheet both give 19 July 2023 as the start of collection for this version. The BMJ Open protocol publication instead states that enrollment began on 18 July 2023 and would continue until 30 November 2026; the higher-ranked FAIRhub value is recorded here.

Non-probability sampling. Contact pools were identified at each site by screening electronic health records for ICD-10 diagnosis codes and demographic data, and invitations were issued in waves whose composition and size were adjusted by under- and oversampling groups as recruitment progressed, with the aim of an equal distribution across four self-reported race/ethnicity groups, biological sex and four diabetes severity categories. All participants who enrolled and completed the protocol within the collection window are included; no instances were excluded at preprocessing.

The cohort is deliberately balanced across race/ethnicity, sex and diabetes severity rather than matched to the demographic distribution of the United States population, because balanced training data are treated as critical for developing unbiased machine learning models.

The FAIRhub healthsheet answers that the dataset contains all possible instances and records "N/A" for sampling strategy, while the FAIRhub study description records the sampling method as a non-probability sample and the BMJ Open protocol describes stratified, wave-based recruitment from an electronic-health-record-derived study base of patients aged 40 and over seen at the three health systems. Both are recorded here: is_sample is set to false with respect to enrolled participants, and the recruitment sampling is described under strategies.

Quality control was applied at the time of data entry and acquisition. Clinical data outside expected minimum/maximum ranges were flagged in REDCap and surfaced in reports reviewed by clinical research coordinators and data managers, who examined the participant record and determined whether an error was likely. Data were checked for credibility against prespecified ranges, incorrect flow through prescribed skip patterns, missing data that could be filled directly from other portions of an individual's record, and the omission or duplication of records. Editing was performed only under the guidance and approval of the site principal investigator; where no logical or appropriate correction existed, the site principal investigator reviewed the values and decided whether to remove them.

The data manager at each collection site was responsible for the quality control of all data before upload to FAIRhub. After transfer to the central project team, the dataset was additionally reviewed internally by AI-READI team members for quality and to confirm that no personally identifiable information had been included.

All data were mapped to applicable standardized terminologies and data standard formats where possible: the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model for clinical data, the Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine standard for retinal imaging, the WaveForm DataBase format for electrocardiography, and Open mHealth for wearable activity and continuous glucose monitoring data.

Device-native formats were converted before upload: Topcon Maestro2 and Triton exports (.fda) and Heidelberg FLIO exports (.sdt) were converted to DICOM, and Garmin exports (.FIT) were converted to the mHealth standard. Electrocardiograms were exported as XML and MoCA results as CSV before conversion.
Processing evolved across releases: version 1.0.0 was produced by custom, ad hoc processing, while versions 2.0.0 and 3.0.0 were produced by a combination of automated and custom processing.

Raw data as exported from the collection devices and from REDCap are retained and expected to be preserved by the AI-READI project at least for the duration of the project, but are not currently shared outside the project team, because they have not been mapped to standardized terminologies and may accidentally include personal health information or personally identifiable information in free-text fields. The project notes the possibility that raw data may be included in future releases of the controlled-access dataset.
Not all modalities are available for all participants; coverage varies by modality rather than being missing at random across the whole record.

Participants electing not to take part in some study elements; collection devices holding no stored results or being returned too late for retrieval (for example a battery that died); data collisions in the processing chain; skipped questions and incomplete responses in surveys; and imaging sessions abandoned because of quality problems.

No imputation was applied. During cleaning, missing values that could be filled directly from other portions of an individual's record were filled; values that could not be logically corrected were reviewed by the site principal investigator for possible removal.
Survey data: skipped questions and incomplete responses are expected.

Wearable device data: improper use and technical failure such as battery failure or system malfunction are expected. The Garmin Vivosmart 5 battery had to be charged every two to three days, so there are gaps in the activity monitoring record.

Imaging data: participant uncooperation, noise that may obscure the images, system malfunction and data transfer failures are expected. Optomed Aurora images are acquired undilated with a handheld camera, so quality varies between participants and within a participant. Heidelberg Spectralis acquisition is operator-dependent and quality issues could lead to a modality being skipped and data missing. FLIO is very sensitive and cannot tolerate more than one centimeter of movement during acquisition; because it is performed last and is uncomfortable, participants may not be at their best compliance.
Participants are volunteers, so the cohort is subject to volunteer bias, which may limit the generalizability of results to people not represented in the study population.
Recruitment was driven from electronic health record screening with personalized mailed and emailed invitations rather than open advertising, and waves were adjusted to correct emerging imbalances.

Recruitment was predominantly urban and hospital-based, which may not capture all cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds, and the cohort does not include other races/ethnicities such as Pacific Islanders and Native Americans. Eligibility required the ability to read and speak English.

Three recording sites were selected for geographic variability across the United States and to broaden representation across racial and ethnic groups, and individuals from all demographic backgrounds were recruited at all three sites.

While the cross-sectional design ultimately aims for balance across race/ethnicity, biological sex and diabetes presence and severity, the pilot release was not balanced across these parameters, and because enrollment is ongoing, periodic interim releases may not have achieved balanced distribution across groups.
Version 3.0.0 as a whole; the recommended validation and test partitions are balanced at 88 participants per race/ethnicity group and 176 per sex, while the training partition is not.

Uniform data collection protocols were implemented for all subjects irrespective of race/ethnicity, biological sex or diabetes severity across all study sites, and the site selection was intended to minimize the potential for sampling bias.

Several measurements are made on more than one device model across the three sites - blood pressure monitors and lensometers differ by site, and retinal imaging is acquired on multiple manufacturers' instruments - so device make and model may be confounded with site.

Information on device make and model, including the specific scan modality used, was documented to ensure repeatability; multiple devices were included deliberately for one measure to enhance generalizability and represent the range of equipment used in clinical settings.

The study cohort may not provide a comprehensive representation of the population: recruitment was predominantly urban and hospital-based, and the cohort does not include Pacific Islanders or Native Americans.
Limits generalization of models derived from the dataset to rural populations and to racial and ethnic groups outside the four recruited.

Eligibility required participants to be able to read and speak English. Non-English speaking participants were not initially enrolled, because translating the consent form alone would not have been sufficient - all study materials and device instructions would have had to be translated.

The project noted that requiring English may have created challenges in recruiting Hispanic and Asian participants and that it would translate materials into Spanish if recruitment goals were not met.

The design is cross-sectional with one study visit per participant, and the ten-day at-home monitoring window is the only longitudinal element in this release. Version 3.0.0 covers only the collection window 19 July 2023 to 1 May 2025, part-way through an enrollment program targeting 4,000 participants.

The public release omits sex, race, ethnicity and medication information, along with 5-digit ZIP code, genetic sequencing data, past health records and traffic and accident reports, which are held under controlled access. Banked biospecimens (plasma, serum, buffy coats, PAXgene RNA tubes and peripheral blood mononuclear cells) are held at the University of Alabama at Birmingham and are not part of the released dataset.
Users of the public release cannot stratify analyses by sex or race/ethnicity, and cannot audit models for disparities across those groups directly.

No labels or targets accompany the dataset and no labeling was performed; the dataset is deliberately hypothesis-agnostic. The project team states it has no formal guidelines for researchers creating new labels or defining new tasks.

Snellen visual acuity variables were dropped in version 3.0.0, so only logMAR visual acuity measurements are available; analyses that depend on Snellen values cannot be carried across from earlier versions.

The dataset does not contain data that might be considered confidential, and no personally identifiable information is included. The RO-Crate records a confidentiality level of HL7:2N (normal) for the release and each of its subcrates.

The RO-Crate enumerates the categories of personal or sensitive information represented in the release as electronic health record data, wearable monitoring, ECG, environmental sensor data, continuous glucose monitor data and wearable accelerometer data.

Two equally ranked tier-1 sources disagree. The RO-Crate enumerates the personal and sensitive information categories recorded above, while the FAIRhub healthsheet answers that the public dataset will not contain data that is considered sensitive and locates racial and ethnic origin, 5-digit ZIP code, genetic sequencing data, past health records, medications and motor vehicle traffic and accident reports in the controlled-access release rather than this one. Because the ranking cannot decide between them, both positions are recorded.
The project's own datasheet answers "No" to whether the dataset contains data that, if viewed directly, might be offensive, insulting, threatening or otherwise pose a safety risk.

The FAIRhub de-identification record classifies the release as NoDeIdentification with direct identifiers and HIPAA identifiers addressed: no identifiers were collected into the released data, so no active de-identification was necessary, but the release was checked to confirm that no data identifiable under US HIPAA were present. The Nature Metabolism comment describes the public set as stripped of Protected Health Information as defined by the HIPAA Privacy Rule via the Safe Harbor method.

Beyond HIPAA identifiers, information related to the sex and race/ethnicity of participants and to medications used has been removed from the public release; 5-digit ZIP code, sex, race, ethnicity, genetic sequencing data, past health records, medications and traffic and accident reports are held under controlled access.

Date shifting, non-arrangement and k-anonymity were not applied. A theoretical risk of future re-identification is acknowledged; to deter re-identification attempts the project implements a data dissemination system, a strict license agreement and data watermarking for both the public and the controlled sets.

Three sources characterize this differently: the FAIRhub structured metadata records the de-identification type as NoDeIdentification with the explanation that no identifiers were collected; the RO-Crate records deidentified as true; and the Nature Metabolism comment describes HIPAA Safe Harbor stripping of the public set. Separately, the University of Washington IRB protocol shows that the study itself collected direct identifiers (name, medical record number, date of birth, address, phone number, email and driver's license number) and linked them to study data by code - none of which are present in the released dataset.

Data watermarking of both the public and controlled sets, a strict license agreement, and a data dissemination system built to deter re-identification. The take-home devices were chosen with participant privacy as a primary concern: the environmental sensor and the Garmin fitness tracker capture no video or audio, carry no GPS location monitoring, and are not synced with participant-owned devices. During the study all procedures were conducted in private rooms and identifiable information was held on encrypted servers or in locked cabinets with restricted access at every site.

A theoretical risk of future re-identification is acknowledged. The license forbids any attempt to identify or contact a data subject, to extract identifying information, or to establish a data subject's membership in a particular group.

Within the release, records are linked only by a study participant identifier; there is one visit per participant and all instances belong to the same project. In the study itself, identifiers and study data were stored separately with a code maintaining the link.

University of Washington Institutional Review Board protocol STUDY00016228. Initial approval was received on 20 December 2022, with reliance agreements covering the Institutional Review Boards of the University of Alabama at Birmingham and the University of California, San Diego. An annual renewal application reporting the status and progress of the study is required and is due within 90 days of expiration.
University of Washington Human Subjects Division; IRB Reliance Team, hsdrely@uw.edu, 4333 Brooklyn Ave NE Box 359470, Seattle, WA 98195-9470, United States.

Human subject review status recorded as submitted and approved. The study is not FDA regulated for either drug or device, has no Data Monitoring Committee, and is not a patient registry. It is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT06002048.

No protected population was targeted. Eligibility was restricted to adults with a minimum age of 40 years and a maximum age of 85 years; pregnancy, gestational diabetes and type 1 diabetes were exclusion criteria.

The RO-Crate names the reviewing body "Washington University IRB" while giving a University of Washington Human Subjects Division postal address and a uw.edu contact, and both publications and the healthsheet attribute the approval to the University of Washington IRB. The healthsheet's eligibility list gives only a lower age bound of 40 years, whereas the FAIRhub study description records a maximum age of 85 years and an exclusion for adults older than 85.

Minors were not enrolled: the minimum age for participation was 40 years. Prisoners were not a target population and the protocol states the research is not likely to have subjects who become prisoners while participating. Pregnancy and gestational diabetes were exclusion criteria. Cognitively impaired adults and other adults unable to consent were not included, so no surrogate consent process applied. Native American or non-US indigenous populations were not actively recruited through a tribe or tribal-focused organization.

Written informed consent, obtained either electronically through REDCap e-consent before the visit or in person at the start of the visit if the participant did not choose electronic consent. The FAIRhub consent record classifies the consent as ConsentSpecifiedNotElsewhereCategorised, with no non-commercial, geographic, research-type, genetic-only or methods restrictions flagged.

The approved consent form for the principal project site, the University of Washington, is published with the dataset documentation at https://docs.aireadi.org/v3/AI-READI%20Consent_Form_Standard_Mod17May2023_useforpilot.pdf. The other clinical sites operated under IRB reliance and used the same consent form with minor institution-specific language incorporated to meet individual institutional requirements. Signed electronic consents were emailed automatically to the participant, and an additional copy could be requested from the study coordinator at any time.

Consent covered participation in the study protocol including questionnaires, collection and banking of blood and urine derivatives for future research, and placement of the resulting data in an open-source repository. Informed consent was required before participation in any part of the protocol.

Potential participants were mailed a hardcopy invitation letter and sent an invitation email, each personalized with links, access codes and QR codes directing them into the study's online REDCap interface. There they could read an overview of the research program, expectations for participation and answers to frequently asked questions; download the informed consent document; request a call back from study staff; complete a screening survey for qualification; and enroll by signing the electronic consent. Participants could reach the e-consent documentation and decide at that point not to participate or to seek additional information. No study-specific questionnaires other than the screening questionnaire were available until consent had been given. Those without internet access could call research staff for alternative methods of enrollment.

Every individual was aware of the data collection: this was active data collection directly from participants, not passive collection or secondary use of existing data. Notification took the form of the personalized invitation letter and email that followed the electronic health record screening, and the consent materials made available through the REDCap interface before any study-specific data were collected.

Participants were permitted to withdraw consent at any time and cease study participation. Any data that had been shared or used up to that point would remain in the dataset; this is clearly communicated in the consent document. Participants were also reminded throughout the study that they had the right to change their mind about participation.
No data protection impact assessment of the dataset and its use on data subjects has been conducted.
