values.text: Bridge2AI-Voice: An ethically-sourced, diverse voice dataset linked to health information
Raw voice, speech and respiratory audio recordings and questionnaire responses collected under the Bridge2AI Voice Data Acquisition protocol and exported from REDCap.

Bridge2AI-Voice is a voice dataset linked to health information, generated by the Bridge2AI-Voice consortium as a Precision Public Health grand challenge project funded by the NIH Common Fund Bridge2AI program. Version 3.1.0 contains data for 833 adult participants recruited across five sites in North America and selected for conditions that manifest within the voice waveform: voice disorders, neurological and neurodegenerative disorders, mood and psychiatric disorders and respiratory disorders, alongside control participants. The release distributes only data considered low risk: features derived from the recorded audio rather than the original waveforms. Derived features include spectrograms, Mel spectrograms, Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, articulatory and source measures from Speech Articulatory Coding, phonetic posteriorgrams, pitch contours, and static acoustic and phonetic measures from openSMILE, Praat and parselmouth. Alongside the features the release provides per-recording metadata and a phenotype directory holding demographics, acoustic confounders, per-condition diagnosis tables, enrollment records, validated questionnaire responses and acoustic task records, each table accompanied by a JSON data dictionary. Recordings were collected in clinic on a custom tablet application with a head-mounted microphone following standardized multi-disorder acoustic protocols, and clinical diagnoses were established by a clinician at the collection site from gold-standard work-up, the electronic health record, or an active prescription. Feature tensors are distributed as Parquet and the phenotype and static feature tables as tab-delimited text. Access is credentialed: users must be PhysioNet credentialed and must sign the Bridge2AI Voice Registered Access Agreement. The original audio waveforms are not part of this release and are disseminated separately under controlled access.

Bensoussan, Y., Sigaras, A., Rameau, A., Elemento, O., Powell, M., Dorr, D., Payne, P., Ravitsky, V., Belisle-Pipon, J., Bahr, R., Watts, S., Bolser, D., Siu, J., Lerner-Ellis, J., Rudzicz, F., Boyer, M., Abdel-Aty, Y., Ahmed Syed, T., Anibal, J., ... Ghosh, S. (2026). Bridge2AI-Voice: An ethically-sourced, diverse voice dataset linked to health information (version 3.1.0). PhysioNet. RRID:SCR_007345. https://doi.org/10.13026/8xbn-nq66
Coordinating and co-lead institution for the Bridge2AI-Voice data generation project, and the institution whose Institutional Review Board approved data collection and sharing.
USF Health Morsani College of Medicine, University of South Florida
The project documentation writes the name as "Yael Bensoussan" with a diaeresis; the PhysioNet author list, preferred here as the higher-ranked source, writes it without one.
Co-lead institution for the Bridge2AI-Voice project, responsible with the University of South Florida for project leadership and for the software and IT infrastructure used in collection.
Englander Institute for Precision Medicine, Weill Cornell Medicine

Multi-institutional, multi-disciplinary consortium that developed the acquisition protocols, collected the data and prepared the release. The consortium gathered experts from North American institutions spanning laryngology, speech-language pathology, acoustic science, neurology, psychiatry, pulmonary science, machine learning, data science, bioethics and social science; the project documentation records over fifty investigators, clinicians, scholars and trainees contributing to the dataset.
National Institutes of Health Common Fund, Bridge2AI Program

Project number given in the PhysioNet acknowledgements for the release, under the project title "Bridge2AI: Voice as a Biomarker of Health - Building an ethically sourced, bioaccoustic database to understand disease like never before".
Core project number recorded by NIH RePORTER, and the organization study identifier given in the project documentation's study metadata.

Sources give different forms of the award identifier. PhysioNet gives 3OT2OD032720-01S1; NIH RePORTER gives application project number 3OT2OD032720-01S3 against core project number OT2OD032720, with a fiscal year 2025 award amount of 4,660,942 and a project period of 2022-09-01 to 2026-11-30; the feasibility publication states "National Institute for Health Grant #1OT2OD032720-01"; the project documentation footer gives the garbled forms "3TF-OT2ActfOD032720Projectf01S1" and "Award #3Tf-OTOD03272001S2". The PhysioNet form is preferred as the highest-ranked source for the release itself.

Maintains PhysioNet, the platform that hosts and distributes this release. PhysioNet is supported by the National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering, the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute and the NIH Office of the Director under grant numbers U24EB037545 and R01EB030362.
Bridge2AI-Voice Consortium Data Access Compliance Office
Curates the dataset and reviews access requests. Requests for the raw audio and questions about access are directed to DACO@b2ai-voice.org.

To create a large, ethically sourced and demographically diverse voice dataset linked to health information, to fuel research and discovery in voice biomarkers and to serve as a foundation for voice AI research.

To enable the development, benchmarking or validation of clinically applicable machine-learning models for diagnosing a wide range of health conditions using voice data, including vocal pathologies and neurological, psychiatric, respiratory and pediatric voice disorders.

To support integration of voice as a biomarker of health into clinical care by linking voice to multimodal health biomarkers and enabling predictive models that assist in screening, diagnosis and treatment of a broad range of diseases.

The absence of large-scale, diverse and well-documented voice data for clinical machine-learning applications. Earlier studies of machine-learning voice diagnosis produced promising results but used sample sizes that were too small, or lacked the key metadata needed to train robust, clinically useful models.
The lack of existing standards for how voice and other acoustic data are measured and collected, which makes comparing studies and pooling data across studies difficult.

The privacy of industry-held voice datasets, which limits the ability to audit machine-learning models and the accuracy of training data labels, and prevents external auditing of training datasets for fair representation of diverse populations.

The scarcity of voice data linked to accurate clinical and demographic information; existing open-source datasets are limited in size, quality and diversity, which the consortium identifies as a reason no validated, FDA-approved voice AI algorithm for disease detection and monitoring has emerged.

Training machine-learning models for disease detection and classification from voice data, using diagnostic labels spanning vocal pathologies, neurological disorders, psychiatric conditions and respiratory disorders.
Pretraining, fine-tuning, benchmarking and validation of AI models for the screening, diagnosis and monitoring of health conditions using voice as a non-invasive, cost-effective biomarker.

Acoustic data were directly observed by recording participants performing standardized tasks, and demographic, confounder and questionnaire data were reported by the participants themselves. Clinical diagnoses were verified by clinicians, who reviewed audio and imaging data, consulted electronic health records, or relied on active medication prescriptions. The released acoustic values are inferred or derived rather than observed directly: they are features computed from the recorded waveforms rather than the waveforms themselves.

Voice samples were collected prospectively with a custom software application running on a tablet, following the Bridge2AI-Voice protocols. A headset with microphone was used where possible. Data were collected on iPads (9th or 10th generation) and iPad Air (5th generation) using an Avid AE-36 microphone connected through an Apple dongle. The application collects breathing and cough sounds, voice, speech and linguistic tasks, and administers demographic surveys, confounder questions and validated questionnaires.

Clinical, diagnostic and questionnaire data were captured in a REDCap database as part of the case report form, and the released tables were exported and converted from REDCap using an open-source library developed by the consortium. The supporting REDCap data dictionary, metadata and instrument PDFs are published separately.
The project documentation records that the data were collected over a period of twelve months. No collection start or end dates are given for this release.
Recruitment, consent and supervised data collection

Research teams, which may include medical, graduate or undergraduate students, coordinated with clinicians and doctors to identify appropriate participants and conducted the collection sessions with the participant in clinic. Hospital staff were not involved in scheduling but assisted with the logistics of coordinating data collection.

Clinicians and doctors at each site were listed under the IRB as co-investigators and were added to the consortium so that their names appear on consortium-level publications. They established or confirmed the diagnostic label for each participant.
Data were collected from the individuals in question directly, in clinic, rather than obtained through third parties. Collection took place in the United States and Canada.

Non-probability sampling. Participants were recruited across academic institutions from high-volume expert clinics on the basis of a diagnosis in one of the five predetermined disease cohort categories, and screened against cohort-specific inclusion and exclusion criteria before their visit by the project investigators. Participants without the conditions of interest were enrolled to serve as controls.

The release is a sample of a larger, ongoing collection. It is not representative because it was collected at a limited number of geographic locations; the consortium states it hopes to improve representativeness by shifting to remote collection and by designing recruitment to control for more variables.

Each participant carries diagnostic labels drawn from the five disease cohort categories, or a control designation. Labels are the result of a clinical assessment: at each site a local clinician provided the diagnosis from a clinical interview and appropriate work-up, and for the psychiatric disorders cohort the assessment was determined from the participant's electronic health record or an active prescription, made outside data collection by an appropriately licensed clinician.
Some questions in the protocol are optional.
Disease-specific questionnaire and diagnosis fields outside a participant's cohort
Each individual answered a common set of questions and then responded to additional questions relevant to their primary diagnostic category.
Isolated fields lost to collection irregularities
Data collection irregularities caused some information to be missing from individual instances.
A participant may have more than one recording session, so a participant may appear on more than one row of a phenotype table, and responses for the same data element need not agree across sessions.
Derived acoustic feature record for one audio recording

Each element carries the participant identifier, the session identifier, the task performed, the number of time frames and the feature tensor. Counts differ by feature because some recordings could not yield some features and because dense features were withheld for sensitive records: 29,278 spectrogram, Mel spectrogram and MFCC records; 32,522 torchaudio pitch records; 28,640 articulatory records; 31,855 loudness records; 31,872 periodicity and Speech Articulatory Coding pitch records; and 29,289 phonetic posteriorgram records.
Questionnaire, demographic, confounder, diagnosis or task response record

Distributed as tab-delimited tables in the phenotype directory, each paired with a JSON data dictionary whose entries carry a description, the question put to the participant where there was one, and the data type of the response.
Age, gender, sex, ethnicity and socioeconomic status are recorded, together with race and sexual orientation.

The dataset has skews based on disorder category, site and other demographic factors; the project documentation advises users to consider the multivariate distribution when assessing utility for a given question.

Disease cohort category. Five categories were defined for the project: voice disorders, neurological and neurodegenerative disorders, mood and psychiatric disorders, respiratory disorders, and pediatric voice and speech disorders.

This adult release covers the first four categories together with controls; the pediatric category is released as a separate dataset. The public data releases do not contain an equal distribution of the disease categories.

Individual participants are unrelated to one another. Within a participant, feature records are linked to sessions and tasks through the participant identifier, session identifier and task name shared across the feature, metadata and phenotype tables; a participant may have more than one session and therefore more than one row in a phenotype table.

No recommended train, validation or test splits are supplied. The project documentation states that researchers are encouraged to create their own data splits according to their specific requirements.
Different sites used different collection configurations, and the collection protocol changed over the course of the study.
Sources of noise in the data include noise artifacts in the recordings, variations in diagnostic practices between sites, inaccurate questionnaire responses and underreporting.
Certain aspects of the data, for example transcription, were generated using off-the-shelf models that have not been audited for correctness.
Some audio files, whether because of length or other issues, could not yield certain features and are therefore absent from the corresponding bundled feature files.

Phenotype data files contain a row for a participant only if at least one column for that participant is not missing. Each individual answered a common set of questions and then responded to additional questions relevant to their primary diagnostic category, so disease-specific fields are systematically absent for participants outside the corresponding cohort.

Some questionnaire items are optional. Data collection irregularities caused some information to be missing from individual instances. Dense features were withheld where the recording was a free speech task or an audio check, and some recordings could not yield some features.

Missing values are left as missing rather than imputed. The dataset was audited internally for missingness and consistency by the data release team, and the audit protocol includes generating missingness tables; a missingness table is distributed with the dataset.

An audit protocol was applied before release: generate missingness tables; check distributions and outliers; check categorical responses against the schema; and run quality control metrics on the audio tasks. For waveforms this covers the amount of silence and the duration, and for speech tasks it compares the speech produced against the intended passage. Version 3.1.0 adds a table of audio quality metrics derived from the recordings.

The healthsheet in the project documentation answers "No" to whether there was any preprocessing for cleaning the data; the audit and quality-control steps described here are recorded elsewhere in the same documentation and in the PhysioNet release notes.
Raw audio was standardized before feature extraction by converting to monaural and resampling to 16 kHz with a Butterworth anti-aliasing filter applied.

Derived features were computed from the standardized audio. Spectrograms were computed with the short-time Fast Fourier Transform using a 25 ms window, a 10 ms hop and a 400-point FFT, then downsampled by a factor of two in the time domain, giving 201 frequency bins. Sixty Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients and a sixty-bin Mel spectrogram were computed with the same parameters. Speech Articulatory Coding produced kinematic traces of six vocal tract articulators as electromagnetic articulography estimates together with loudness, periodicity and pitch at 50 Hz. Phonetic posteriorgrams give a distribution over forty phoneme categories at 100 Hz. Static acoustic, phonetic and prosodic features were extracted with openSMILE, and with Praat through parselmouth, and pitch contours with torchaudio. Transcriptions were generated with OpenAI's Whisper Large model. Processing was performed with the b2aiprep library, version 3.0.0 for this release, and the senselab audio processing toolkit.

Raw audio files and the questionnaire data retrieved from ReproSchema-UI or exported from REDCap were converted to be compliant with the Brain Imaging Data Structure version 1.9.0, organizing them into a phenotype directory of confounder, demographic, diagnosis, enrollment, questionnaire and task tables alongside per-participant, per-session audio.

The BIDS conversion is described in the project documentation's data pre-processing section, which sets out the folder layout of the audio dataset; the PhysioNet record for version 3.1.0 does not restate it.

The source data are the original audio waveforms recorded through the Bridge2AI-Voice tablet application and the questionnaire and clinical data captured in REDCap. The raw audio is not part of this release: the PhysioNet project contains derived features only. Raw audio, post de-identification, is retained and disseminated separately under controlled access, and requires institutional sign-off.

Diagnostic labels are the result of a clinical assessment of the participant. At each site a local clinician provided the diagnosis based on a clinical interview and appropriate work-up. For the psychiatric disorders cohort the assessment was determined from the participant's electronic health record or an active prescription, carried out outside data collection by an appropriately licensed clinician. Cohort-specific gold-standard validation methods were specified in the protocol, including laryngoscopy images and stroboscopy videos for voice disorders, spirometry and flow volume loops for airway stenosis and chronic cough, brain CT and MRI for the neurological cohort, and the electronic health summary, a psychiatrist's clinical diagnosis and medication history for the mood and psychiatric cohort.
Typically the clinician at the site of data collection, or a clinician external to the study who made a prior diagnostic assessment. A single labeler labeled each instance.

Labeling followed the Bridge2AI protocols and ICD-10 codes. The project documentation recommends that any new labels be described alongside the release of a model or publication, including the exact variables used for the determination.
Labels were recorded in REDCap through the Bridge2AI-Voice case report form.

Whisper Large generated the transcriptions of the recordings. openSMILE captured temporal dynamics and acoustic characteristics as static features per recording. Praat and parselmouth provided phonetic and prosodic measures including fundamental frequency, formants and voice quality. torchaudio produced spectrograms, Mel spectrograms, MFCCs and pitch contours. Speech Articulatory Coding produced electromagnetic articulography estimates for six articulators together with loudness, periodicity and pitch. The ppgs package produced phonetic posteriorgrams, a time-varying categorical distribution over forty acoustic units of speech at 100 Hz. b2aiprep organized and preprocessed the dataset and merged the source data into the phenotype files; senselab processed the audio files for research tasks.
Certain aspects of the data, for example transcription, were generated using off-the-shelf models that have not been audited for correctness.
Unique identifier for the participant, present in every feature and phenotype table.
Unique identifier for the recording session. A participant may have more than one session.
The acoustic task performed for the recording from which the feature was derived.
The number of time frames associated with a time-varying feature for that recording.

Derived acoustic features. Nine dense binary files in Parquet format hold the time-varying features: ppgs.parquet, sparc_ema.parquet, sparc_loudness.parquet, sparc_periodicity.parquet, sparc_pitch.parquet, torchaudio_spectrogram.parquet, torchaudio_mfcc.parquet, torchaudio_pitch.parquet and torchaudio_mel_spectrogram.parquet. Two plain-text files hold per-recording values: static_features.tsv, one feature per audio recording, and audio_quality_metrics.tsv, quality control metrics per recording. Each file is accompanied by a JSON data dictionary sharing its file stem.
A Parquet file and its data dictionary carrying per-recording information, including the task instructions and prompts and the microphone used with its gain.

Information collected from the participant or another individual during the encounter, organized into subdirectories: confounders; demographics; diagnosis, holding a table per condition covering airway stenosis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, anxiety, benign lesions, bipolar disorder, cognitive impairment, control, COPD and asthma, depression, glottic insufficiency, laryngeal cancer, laryngeal dystonia, laryngitis, muscle tension dysphonia, Parkinson's disease, precancerous lesions, unexplained chronic cough and unilateral vocal fold paralysis; enrollment, holding eligibility, enrollment form and participant tables; questionnaire, holding the ADHD adult, custom affect scale, DSM-5 adult, dyspnea index, GAD-7, Leicester cough questionnaire, PANAS, PHQ-9, productive vocabulary, psychiatric history, PTSD adult, VHI-10 and voice perception tables; and task, holding acoustic task, Harvard sentences, random item generation, recording, session, Stroop and Winograd tables. Every table is tab-delimited and paired with a JSON data dictionary.
Dense binary feature files are made available as Parquet, an open-source column-oriented data file format, and can be loaded with any library that supports Parquet.
Tab-separated values with JSON data dictionaries

Phenotype tables, static features and audio quality metrics are distributed as tab-delimited plain text. Each table has a companion JSON data dictionary whose keys match the column names of the table.
Version 1.0 was published earlier on the Health Data Nexus platform rather than on PhysioNet.

The dataset is distributed broadly to individuals outside the entity that created it, through PhysioNet, under credentialed access with a signed data use agreement. Raw audio is shared with external institutions only through controlled access, after review by the Data Access Compliance Office and execution of a Data Transfer and Use Agreement signed by an authorized official of the recipient institution.

Files are released under the Bridge2AI Voice Registered Access License. Only credentialed users who sign the Bridge2AI Voice Registered Access Agreement may access the files; no additional training is required. Registered access to the feature-only data requires registration on PhysioNet, confirmation of identity, and signature of the Registered Access Agreement. Controlled access to the raw audio requires a Data Access Request Form, a Data Use Agreement, a review by the Data Access Compliance Office, and a Data Use and Transfer Agreement signed by an authorized official at the applicant's institution. The dataset is intended solely for commercial and non-commercial research purposes by Authorized Researchers; the consent does not restrict use to non-commercial purposes, to a geographic location, to a type of research, to genetic research, or away from methods and algorithm development. Collaborators at other research organizations, and other research teams at the same organization, must apply independently for access and sign their own Data Transfer and Use Agreement.

The data may be protected by copyright and other rights, including other intellectual property rights; nothing in the agreement transfers any intellectual property rights in or relating to the data to the recipient.
Duplication as reasonably required to carry out the research project with the data is permitted; sale of all or part of the data on any media is not permitted.

Users agree not to make intellectual property claims on the data, and not to use intellectual property protection in ways that would prevent or block access to, or use of, any element of the data or conclusions drawn directly from it.

Users who perform further research adding intellectual and resource capital may obtain intellectual property rights on downstream discoveries, but agree to implement licensing policies that will not obstruct further research, and to respect the Fort Lauderdale Agreement.
No intellectual-property-based restrictions have been imposed by third parties on the data associated with the instances.
No export controls apply to the dataset.
Access is restricted to credentialed users who have signed the Bridge2AI Voice Registered Access Agreement; raw audio requires institutional sign-off under a Data Transfer and Use Agreement.

The data are covered by a Certificate of Confidentiality, which must be asserted against compulsory legal demands such as court orders and subpoenas for identifying information or characteristics of a research participant. The Data Transfer and Use Agreement records that the data are personally identifiable information as defined in OMB Memorandum M-07-16, and obliges recipients to adhere to the specific requirements of PhysioNet.
University of South Florida Board of Trustees

Two routes exist. For the feature-only data, a prospective user registers on PhysioNet, confirms their identity as a credentialed user, and signs the Bridge2AI Voice Registered Access Agreement. For the raw audio, which is disseminated through controlled access only to protect participants' privacy, the applicant completes a Data Access Request Form and a Data Use Agreement and submits the application to the Data Access Compliance Office for review; on approval, a Data Use and Transfer Agreement must be signed by an authorized official at the applicant's institution. Access to raw audio is a more involved process requiring institutional sign-off, and requests are directed to the access committee at DACO@b2ai-voice.org. Recipients must retain control over the data, must not disclose or grant access to any third party other than the authorized persons named in the agreement, and must store the data with administrative, physical and technical safeguards adequate to protect personally identifiable information.
Provider Institution: the University of South Florida Board of Trustees provides the data under the Data Transfer and Use Agreement.
Recipient Scientist and Recipient Authorized Institutional Official: named in each Data Transfer and Use Agreement, and responsible for the recipient institution's compliance.
Authorized Persons: recipient faculty, employees, fellows, students and agents listed in the agreement and bound to equivalent standards of confidentiality and security.
Within the collecting institutions, only the principal investigator and the study team have access to medical records, REDCap records and identifiable clinical information.

A memorandum setting out the ethical justification for controlled access to raw voice data samples is published alongside the project documentation, explaining the reasoning behind the governance structure.

The project documentation's healthsheet answers "No" to whether the dataset contains data that might be considered confidential, such as data protected by legal privilege or by doctor-patient confidentiality, or the content of individuals' non-public communications.

This answer is recorded against the released feature-only dataset. The raw audio, which is not part of this release, is held under controlled access precisely because of its re-identification potential.

The dataset includes race and ethnic origin information, sexual orientation information, and socioeconomic and health information. Voice itself is a biometric characteristic; the derived features are released in place of the waveform for that reason.

The same documentation records that all fields encoded as sensitive in the REDCap data dictionary were removed at the version 3.0.0 release stage, along with non-identifying elements revealing highly sensitive information such as household income, mental health status and traumatic life experiences. The healthsheet's inventory of sensitive content and the de-identification section's account of what was removed are therefore not fully consistent; both are reported here.

The dataset includes the transcription of free speech tasks. While the inclusion of offensive, insulting or threatening material is unlikely, it cannot be completely avoided, as research participants are responsible for their choice of language.

This warning is recorded in the project documentation's healthsheet. Transcripts of free speech audio were removed at the version 1.1 release, and dense features derived from free speech audio were excluded from versions 3.0.0 and 3.1.0, so the residual exposure in the current release is narrower than the warning as written.
HIPAA Safe Harbor de-identification, supplemented by removal of indirect identifiers and of highly sensitive non-identifying elements, and by withholding the raw audio waveform.

names geographic locators date information at a resolution finer than years phone and fax numbers email addresses IP addresses Social Security Numbers medical record numbers health plan beneficiary numbers device identifiers license numbers account numbers vehicle identifiers website URLs full face photographs biometric identifiers any other unique identifiers state and province, with country of data collection retained

All direct identifiers were removed as they would reveal the identity of the research participant, including name, civic address and social security numbers. Indirect identifiers were removed where they created a significant risk of re-identification through combination with other public data available on social media, in government registries or elsewhere; these include selected geographic and demographic identifiers and some information about household composition or cultural identity. Non-identifying elements revealing highly sensitive information, such as household income, mental health status and traumatic life experiences, were also removed. All raw voice data was withheld because of its potential to cause re-identification or to be used for illicit or unauthorized purposes; only extracted features are released. Raw audio transcripts were reviewed and any recordings containing potentially identifying information or external voices were removed from the release. Spectrograms, Mel spectrograms, MFCCs, phonetic posteriorgrams and articulatory estimates were excluded for sensitive records, for audio checks and where the audio contained free speech; static and other features that do not encode the sensitive information were retained. Direct identifiers were removed, HIPAA de-identification rules were applied, dates were rebased or replaced by integers, geographic information was removed or generalized, and narrative text fields were removed; k-anonymization with k of at least two was not achieved.
Removal of HIPAA Safe Harbor identifiers and of selected indirect and highly sensitive fields, combined with release of derived acoustic features in place of the original waveforms.

Withholding of raw audio, released only under controlled access. Manual review of transcripts and removal of recordings containing identifying information or external voices. Storage of identifiable data within the collecting institution on password-protected REDCap databases behind the institutional HIPAA firewall, with access limited to approved study personnel who have completed HIPAA and privacy training. Transmission of collected data over a secure HTTPS protocol to HIPAA-compliant cloud storage provided through NIH STRIDES partners.

The protocol records that even after removing all HIPAA-protected information, a person's voice is unique to them and to their health at that time, so it is always possible, even if unlikely, that someone could recognize a participant by voice. The published release mitigates this by excluding the waveform. Users are prohibited from attempting re-identification.

Participants who consent permit investigators to access medical information through electronic health record platforms in order to perform gold-standard validation of diagnoses and symptoms. Identifiable data and the datasheets linking participant numbers to participant information are kept within each collecting institution and are not shared.
University of South Florida Institutional Review Board

Data collection and sharing was approved by the University of South Florida Institutional Review Board. The clinical study was submitted to and approved by the USF Single IRB and by subsite IRBs through the Single IRB process. The study is not for a drug product or a medical device, and no data monitoring committee was appointed.
HIPAA; a Certificate of Confidentiality covering the data; the Single IRB process for United States sites, with separate research ethics board review for the Canadian sites.
Participants with neurological and neurodegenerative diagnoses including mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease, other dementias, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and Parkinson's disease.
Participants with mood and psychiatric diagnoses including depression, bipolar disorder, anxiety, PTSD and ADHD.
The approved protocol provides for signed assent for children or for adults unable to consent, alongside signed, verbal and electronic consent options for adults able to consent.

Pediatric participants were enrolled only through the pediatric sites and not at the coordinating site; the adult study population is restricted to participants aged 18 years and older, with a maximum age of 120.

Where children participate in the wider project, parents or guardians provide consent and children provide assent where appropriate; permission from one parent or legal guardian suffices because the research is minimal risk. Pediatric enrollment is outside this adult dataset.

Prospective written informed consent. Participants may consent by signing a physical paper copy, by indicating electronic consent within the application or through REDCap surveys, or through a video recording within the application in which the participant reads a statement aloud, which also serves to verify that the acoustic data submitted belongs to the consented individual.
Paper consent documents are uploaded and saved electronically in REDCap. All paper and electronic versions of consent are stored for a minimum of five years after completion of the study.

Research data that does not contain direct identifiers will be shared with external researchers for future research through a secure database. Data posing a low risk of re-identification is shared in registered access with the general public; data that would pose a heightened risk if shared in full open access is shared through a controlled access mechanism with authorized researchers. Participants who consent also permit investigators to access medical information through electronic health record platforms for gold-standard validation of diagnoses and symptoms. For longitudinal collection, an electronic consent is administered before each subsequent collection to confirm ongoing consent.

Participants are informed that they may withdraw from the study at any point. If a participant withdraws during or before the voice data collection is completed, their data will not be included in the database. Participants are informed that research data, including voice recordings, cannot be removed from the database once the voice data collection process is complete.

All participants were duly informed and agreed to the collection and use of their data via prospective informed consent, obtained through an IRB-approved consent process before any data was collected.

Individuals were notified about the data collection: participants went through an IRB-approved consent process in which they were informed of what data was being collected, the methods used to secure it and how it would be used.

Consenting participants are informed that they may withdraw from the study at any point. If a participant chooses to withdraw during or before the voice data collection, their data will not be included in the database. Participants are informed that research data, including voice recordings, cannot be removed from the database once the voice data collection process has been completed. For longitudinal cohorts, participants may decide to withdraw at any point during the study period, and data already collected is retained.
University of South Florida Institutional Review Board

Data collection and sharing was reviewed and approved by the University of South Florida Institutional Review Board. United States participating institutions joined through the Single IRB process, with subsite IRB approvals obtained under that process.
Canadian participating institutions' research ethics boards

The protocol records that the Canadian institutions do not follow the Single IRB process and apply for separate research ethics board approval to comply with Canadian regulations, with a copy of the approved application submitted to the coordinating IRB. Genomic data collection and analysis, conducted only at the Canadian sites, is covered by a separate protocol and is not part of this release.
40 US dollars for a data collection session lasting under 90 minutes and 80 US dollars for a session lasting over 90 minutes, for no more than three sessions and a maximum total of 120 US dollars.
The compensation scheme changed over the life of the protocol; the amounts recorded here are those given in the project documentation and in the current protocol revision.

Development, benchmarking or validation of clinically applicable machine-learning models for diagnosing health conditions from voice, including vocal pathologies and neurological, psychiatric, respiratory and pediatric voice disorders.
The dataset is structured to be findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable, and contains voice-derived recordings together with key metadata.
Pretraining or fine-tuning of models on derived acoustic features.
Research on the use of voice as a non-invasive, cost-effective biomarker for the screening, diagnosis and monitoring of a wide range of health conditions.
The dataset is intended strictly for research that prioritizes patient safety, privacy and ethical use.
A restricted version of the dataset containing raw audio was used in the Bridge2AI Summer School and hackathon.
Training opportunities for using the dataset are offered through the Bridge2AI Voice Scholars program.

Non-research applications are discouraged, including hiring decisions, insurance premium adjustments and any form of surveillance that could lead to discrimination or harm. These limits are intended to prevent unethical or biased outcomes that could negatively affect individuals on the basis of their health conditions or voice characteristics.

Uses that assume the dataset is representative are discouraged. The dataset carries skews by disorder category, site and demographic factors, and users should consider the multivariate distribution when assessing utility for a given question.
Attempting to re-identify research participants, or taking any action that could reasonably lead to re-identification, is prohibited under the Registered Access Agreement.
Any purpose that could foreseeably cause harm or stigmatization to research participants, their families, communities or specific populations is prohibited.

Intellectual property protections, database rights or related rights may not be used in a manner that restricts or limits access to any part of the dataset or to any conclusions derived from it, so that future use of the dataset remains unrestricted in alignment with the consortium's Open Science principles.

Recipients may not use the data, alone or in concert with other information, to make any effort to contact the individuals who are the subjects of the data without appropriate Institutional Review Board approval, specific written approval from the provider, and informed consent from the individual where required.

The dataset carries skews based on disorder category, site and other demographic factors, and on the way it was collected, cleaned and labeled. A future user should consider the multivariate distribution when assessing utility for a given question, to avoid unfair treatment of individuals or groups through stereotyping or quality-of-service failures.

Because labels reflect diagnoses made under varying clinical practices at different sites, and because collection devices and configurations differ by site and therefore by cohort, models trained on the data may learn site or device signatures rather than disease signatures.
Groups that have less trust in the medical system or in AI, or that are less proximal to the collection sites, would have been less likely to be recruited.
The consortium states it hopes to make the data more representative by shifting to remote collection and by designing the recruitment approach to control for more variables.

The sample was collected at a limited number of geographic locations, across five recording sites in the United States and Canada, and is limited to fluent English speakers. It is therefore not representative of the larger population from which it is drawn.
The project documentation states that collection will expand to include Spanish, and that remote collection is planned.

Participants were screened for different disorders based on site, so cohorts also had their data collected on different devices; distinct iPad devices were used at each site. Recordings were made with a head-mounted headset whose microphone distance could vary slightly between participants, and the clinical diagnosis was made by a single clinician or from an electronic health record or prescription depending on the disorder.
Disease cohort categories, which are confounded with collection site and device.

Each instance carries a single diagnostic label from a single labeler, and diagnostic practices vary between sites, so label quality is not uniform across cohorts. The human-level performance of the diagnostic task varies widely across the conditions covered.
The dataset covers fluent English speakers only. Individuals who do not read or speak English were excluded from data collection for the released versions.
Spanish-language protocols and collection are described as under development for future releases.

The project documentation gives English as the only language option for version 2.0.0; later revisions of the IRB protocol permit English or Spanish speakers, but no Spanish data is described in the released versions.
The release is a non-probability sample of a larger, ongoing collection, drawn from high-volume expert clinics at five sites, and is not representative of the wider population.
Models trained on the release may not generalize to populations, settings or recording conditions unlike those sampled.
The release contains only data considered low risk: derivations such as spectrograms, and not the original voice recordings. Analyses requiring the waveform cannot be run on this release.
Raw audio is available separately under controlled access, requiring institutional sign-off and review by the Data Access Compliance Office.
The collection protocol changed over the course of the study, and changes in diagnostic criteria or practices over time could be a source of distribution shift within the dataset.

The public data releases do not contain an equal distribution of the five disease categories, and this adult release omits the pediatric category entirely. Multimodal data described in the protocol, including imaging, genomic data and respiratory function tests, is not part of this release.

Version 3.1.0 fixed broken Parquet files carried over from the previous release, and updated validated diagnosis information across conditions with back-filled information. Some phenotype files were rearranged and certain gold standard variable names were renamed.
Version 2.0 reprocessed the spectrograms to fix minor issues identified in the previous release, and removed all spectrograms and Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients derived from free speech files.

The project documentation states that there is no erratum and that a changelog for each dataset version is published online with the dataset metadata; the corrections recorded here are drawn from the PhysioNet release notes.
Semi-annual, that is twice a year.

Further versions of the dataset are released as new versions rather than in-place edits, each with its own DOI. Users are notified through news items on the hosting platform and through standard communication channels. Successive releases have added participants, added derived features, reorganized the file layout and corrected errors; the dataset itself is released as static versions rather than being dynamically updated.
The semi-annual cadence and notification arrangements are stated in the project documentation against hosting on the Health Data Nexus platform; the current release is hosted on PhysioNet.
1.0 - first release of the Bridge2AI voice as a biomarker of health dataset, published on Health Data Nexus, providing 12,523 recordings for 306 participants.
2.0.0, 16 April 2025 - added 136 new participants; spectrograms reprocessed; free-speech spectrograms and MFCCs removed.
2.0.1, 18 August 2025 - corrections to the authorship list.
3.0.0, 16 December 2025 - added 391 new participants; the single phenotype file separated into individual files; articulatory and phonetic posteriorgram features added; files reorganized.
3.1.0, 1 May 2026 - no new participants, but additional data released for certain participants; broken Parquet files fixed; audio quality metrics and per-recording metadata added.

Each version has a unique DOI, and a concept DOI resolves to the latest version. Older versions remain listed on PhysioNet, but the files for version 1.1 are no longer available. The project documentation states that by default older versions continue to be supported, hosted and made available to researchers, and that the dataset publishers reserve the right to remove access to older versions.
Indefinite for the hosted dataset; two years from the start date for recipients under a Data Transfer and Use Agreement.

Once data is contributed, it will be retained as long as it is useful for research purposes, possibly indefinitely. Recipients under the Data Transfer and Use Agreement must destroy the data two years after the start date, on completion of the project, on termination, or on expiration of the applicable ethics approval, whichever occurs first, and must certify the destruction in writing within thirty days; a single copy may be retained where records retention requirements or research integrity and verification demand it. Within the collecting institutions, identifiable data and the datasheets linking participant numbers to participant information are kept on local cloud storage for a maximum of ten years after study completion and then destroyed.

Others may publish a derivative dataset on the hosting platform that references the original source, made available under the same conditions as the source data. For the code used to produce the data, the open-source repositories have discussion forums and issue pages allowing public discussion of the preprocessing, and accept pull requests contributing improvements to the preprocessing code.
Bridge2AI-Voice project documentation, including the protocols, healthsheet, study metadata and AI-readiness assessment: https://docs.b2ai-voice.org/
b2aiprep, the library used to organize and preprocess the dataset and to merge the source data into the phenotype files, released under Apache-2.0: https://github.com/sensein/b2aiprep
senselab, used to process the audio files for research tasks: https://github.com/sensein/senselab
Bridge2AI REDCap data dictionary, metadata and instrument PDFs, released under MIT: https://github.com/eipm/bridge2ai-redcap
Source code for the documentation site and dashboards, released under MIT: https://github.com/eipm/bridge2ai-docs

The project documentation's healthsheet states that the dataset is self-contained and answers "not applicable" to whether external resources are guaranteed to exist and remain constant over time. The resources listed here are supporting materials and code rather than dependencies of the released files.
Access to the raw audio through Synapse requires review by the Data Access Compliance Office and a signed Data Transfer and Use Agreement.
Recipients further agree to adhere to the specific requirements of PhysioNet, maintained by the MIT Laboratory for Computational Physiology.
Bridge2AI-Voice Pediatric Dataset, version 1.1.0, PhysioNet, DOI 10.13026/h995-bt35

The companion pediatric cohort of the same project, released separately under credentialed access. Version 1.1.0 contains derived audio features for 23,533 recordings collected from 300 participants aged 2 to 18 at the Hospital for Sick Children, using ReproSchema-UI with the Bridge2AI-Voice pediatric protocol. Its collection and sharing was approved by the Research Ethics Board at the Hospital for Sick Children. Version 1.1.0 released no new participants but added audio features for free speech tasks that were manually checked for unconsented speakers and personally identifying information, along with audio quality metrics and per-recording metadata. Raw pediatric audio is available under controlled access via Synapse at https://www.synapse.org/Synapse:syn73617068
Bridge2AI-Voice: An ethically-sourced, diverse voice dataset linked to health information, version 3.0.0, PhysioNet, DOI 10.13026/k81f-qr68
The immediately preceding release, published 16 December 2025, also covering 833 participants.
Bridge2AI-Voice: An ethically-sourced, diverse voice dataset linked to health information, all versions, DOI 10.13026/37yb-1t42
Bridge2AI-Voice raw audio recordings for the adult cohort, distributed under controlled access via Synapse (syn72370534)
The released features are computed from these recordings; the recordings themselves are not part of this release.

The project documentation reports a self-assessment of the dataset against the Bridge2AI AI-readiness recommendations, scoring FAIRness 100 percent, Provenance 100 percent, Characterization 80 percent with the data quality criterion not met, Pre-model explainability 100 percent, Ethics 100 percent, Sustainability 50 percent with the domain-appropriate and associated criteria not met, and Computability 75 percent with the contextualized criterion not met. The consortium's stated collection target exceeds the released cohort: the project documentation describes a flagship dataset of 10,000 voices, with anticipated enrollment of 10,000 by 2027, against 833 adult participants in this release. The study design is recorded as an observational cohort study with a cross-sectional time perspective, enrolling participants of all sexes aged 18 to 120 including healthy volunteers, under organization study identifier OT2OD032720.

The declared source ranking was applied. The PhysioNet record for version 3.1.0 is the primary source and, per the declared ranking, supersedes the PhysioNet record for version 3.0.0; the project documentation, the IRB protocol and the Data Transfer and Use Agreement supply governance, collection and healthsheet detail; the feasibility publication and the audiomics white paper, and the NIH RePORTER page, were used only where higher-ranked sources are silent. Several figures differ between sources. Participant counts: PhysioNet reports 833 participants for both 3.0.0 and 3.1.0, while the project documentation describes version 3.0 as containing approximately 61,937 voice-derived recordings from 833 adult participants; no total recording count is stated for 3.1.0, and the per-feature record counts in the release cannot be summed to one because they count overlapping recordings. Collection target: the project documentation states a flagship dataset of 10,000 voices and anticipated enrollment of 10,000 by 2027, the audiomics white paper states a primary deliverable of a publicly available database of 30,000 human voices, and the IRB protocol states a sample size of 30,000 participants; the project documentation was preferred as the higher-ranked source and the others are recorded here. Grant identifiers differ and are set out in the funders entry. Language eligibility differs: the project documentation records English as the only option for version 2.0.0 with Spanish protocols under development, while later revisions of the IRB protocol permit English or Spanish speakers. Several healthsheet answers in the project documentation are written against version 2.0.0 or 3.0.0 and against hosting on the Health Data Nexus platform rather than PhysioNet; these were carried over only where the tier 1 sources do not contradict them, and the slots concerned carry their own caveats. Contact email addresses in the project documentation were redacted in the source bundle; the access committee address recorded here is the one stated in the PhysioNet news items.

values.text: Bridge2AI-Voice: An ethically-sourced, diverse voice dataset linked to health information

Raw voice, speech, breath and cough audio recordings, together with questionnaire responses retrieved from ReproSchema-UI or exported from REDCap, collected prospectively from consented participants by the Bridge2AI-Voice consortium.

Bridge2AI-Voice is a collection of derived acoustic features and linked health information generated from voice, speech, breath and cough recordings of 833 adult participants enrolled at five clinical sites in the United States and Canada. Participants were selected on the basis of conditions expected to manifest in the voice waveform, drawn from four adult disease cohorts - voice disorders, neurological and neurodegenerative disorders, mood and psychiatric disorders, and respiratory disorders - together with controls. Each participant completed a standardized protocol of acoustic tasks, demographic and confounder surveys, disease-specific validated questionnaires and clinician-confirmed diagnosis, delivered through a custom application running on a tablet with a headset microphone. Version 3.1.0, published on PhysioNet, releases only material assessed as low risk: spectrograms, Mel spectrograms, Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, articulatory and phonetic posteriorgram features, static acoustic features, audio quality metrics, per-recording metadata, and phenotype tables covering demographics, confounders, diagnosis, enrollment, questionnaires and task responses. Raw audio waveforms are withheld from this release and disseminated separately under controlled access. The dataset is the flagship data-generation deliverable of the Precision Public Health grand challenge funded by the NIH Common Fund Bridge2AI program, whose stated aim is to make voice usable as a biomarker of health by supplying a large, diverse and ethically sourced resource for voice artificial-intelligence research.

Bensoussan, Y., Sigaras, A., Rameau, A., Elemento, O., Powell, M., Dorr, D., Payne, P., Ravitsky, V., Belisle-Pipon, J., Bahr, R., Watts, S., Bolser, D., Siu, J., Lerner-Ellis, J., Rudzicz, F., Boyer, M., Abdel-Aty, Y., Ahmed Syed, T., Anibal, J., ... Ghosh, S. (2026). Bridge2AI-Voice: An ethically-sourced, diverse voice dataset linked to health information (version 3.1.0). PhysioNet. RRID:SCR_007345. https://doi.org/10.13026/8xbn-nq66

Multi-institutional consortium that designed the data acquisition protocols, collected the data and prepared the release. The PhysioNet author list for version 3.1.0 names more than one hundred contributors across the participating sites.

To create an ethically sourced flagship dataset of voice recordings linked to health information, so that voice can be developed as a biomarker of health and integrated into clinical care.

To enable the development, benchmarking or validation of clinically applicable machine-learning models for diagnosing a wide range of health conditions from voice, including vocal pathologies and neurological, psychiatric, respiratory and pediatric voice disorders.

To introduce and standardize the field of audiomics by developing new standards of acoustic and voice data collection and analysis, creating benchmarks of diversity metrics, and minimizing the risk of algorithmic bias.
To supply an openly documented resource that supports ethical and trustworthy voice AI research, including guidance on consent, data sharing and privacy safeguards for voice data.

Previous studies of machine-learning voice diagnosis produced promising results but used sample sizes that were too small, or lacked the key metadata needed for training robust, clinically useful models.

Comparing studies and pooling data has been difficult because of the absence of standards for how voice and other acoustic data are measured and collected; the dataset supplies a standardized, protocol-driven collection.

Industry holds large volumes of voice data but lacks accurate clinical and demographic annotation, and those datasets are private, which prevents external auditing of training data for fair representation of diverse populations.

Detection and classification of disease from voice, speech, breath and cough, across vocal pathologies, neurological and neurodegenerative disorders, mood and psychiatric disorders, and respiratory disorders.
Screening, diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring of health conditions using voice as a non-invasive, low-cost biomarker.
Methodological work on acoustic feature extraction, voice bioinformatics standards and diversity benchmarking for voice AI.

Demographic sub-populations are identified by age, gender, sex, ethnicity and socioeconomic status, collected through a detailed demographic questionnaire delivered in the collection application.

The distribution across sub-populations is uneven. The collection is a non-probability sample drawn at five sites; groups with less trust in the medical system or in AI, and groups less proximal to the collection sites, were less likely to be recruited. Participants were screened for different disorders depending on site, so demographic composition, disorder category and recording device are entangled.

Participants with laryngeal and phonatory conditions, including laryngeal cancer, laryngitis, pre-cancerous lesions, benign lesions of the vocal cord, muscle tension dysphonia, spasmodic dysphonia and laryngeal tremor, unilateral vocal fold paralysis, and glottic insufficiency or presbyphonia. Diagnoses are validated against laryngoscopy images and stroboscopy videos, with CT and spirometry for selected diagnoses.

Participants with airway stenosis at supraglottic, glottic, posterior glottic, subglottic, tracheal or multi-level sites, bilateral vocal fold paralysis, and unexplained chronic cough of more than eight weeks, together with COPD and asthma. Diagnoses are validated against spirometry and flow volume loops and CT of the neck and chest.

Participants aged over 44 and under 85 with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease, other dementias, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis or Parkinson's disease. Diagnoses are validated against brain CT and MRI, with serum p-tau biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease and whole genome sequencing where available.

Participants with anxiety disorder, bipolar disorder, or depression and major depressive disorder as index diagnoses, with co-morbid conditions recorded including alcohol or substance use disorder, ADHD, autism spectrum disorder, borderline personality disorder, eating disorder, insomnia or sleep disorder, OCD, panic disorder, PTSD, schizophrenia and social anxiety disorder. Diagnoses are validated from the electronic health summary, a clinical diagnosis from a psychiatrist, and medication history.

Participants not diagnosed with or treated for a voice, respiratory, mood or neurological disorder affecting voice, cough, breath or speech, enrolled to serve as controls. Healthy volunteers are eligible.

Raw audio was preprocessed by converting to monaural and resampling to 16 kHz with a Butterworth anti-aliasing filter applied.

Spectrograms were computed from the standardized audio using the short-time Fast Fourier Transform with a 25 ms window size, 10 ms hop length and a 400-point FFT, and were further downsampled by a factor of two in the time domain after derivation. Sixty Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients and a 60-bin Mel spectrogram were derived with the same parameters.

Articulatory features were generated using the Speech Articulatory Coding package, producing kinematic traces of vocal tract articulators and source features together with loudness, periodicity and pitch measures, all gathered at 50 Hz. Phonetic posteriorgrams giving a time-varying categorical distribution over acoustic units of speech were generated at 100 Hz.

Acoustic features were extracted using openSMILE, capturing temporal dynamics and acoustic characteristics, and phonetic and prosodic features were computed using Parselmouth and Praat, providing measures of fundamental frequency, formants and voice quality.
Transcriptions were generated using the OpenAI Whisper Large model. Transcripts of free speech audio were removed before release.

Raw audio files and questionnaire data retrieved from ReproSchema-UI or exported from REDCap were converted to be compliant with the Brain Imaging Data Structure version 1.9.0, with per-participant and per-session directories holding WAV files and accompanying JSON sidecars, and a phenotype directory holding tab-delimited tables.

The BIDS conversion is described for the audio-plus-questionnaire distribution; the PhysioNet featurized release is organized into features, metadata and phenotype folders rather than the BIDS layout.

No pre-processing was performed for the purpose of cleaning the data, and no instances were excluded at the time of preprocessing. Quality control instead takes the form of an audit protocol run over the release: generating missingness tables, checking distributions and outliers, checking categorical responses against the schema, and running quality control metrics on audio tasks, including the amount of silence, the duration, and for speech tasks a comparison of the produced speech against the intended passage. Processing is performed with the b2aiprep and SenseLab toolkits. Version 3.1.0 adds a file of per-recording audio quality metrics.

Diagnostic labels are the result of a clinical assessment of the participant. At each site, a local clinician provided the diagnosis based on a clinical interview and appropriate work-up. For the psychiatric disorders cohort the assessment was determined from the participant's electronic health record or an active prescription, outside of data collection, by an appropriately licensed clinician. The strategy is described as a gold standard label available in the data.
Bridge2AI protocols and ICD-10 codes, with disorder-specific gold standard validation methods set out in the cohort inclusion and exclusion criteria.

Typically the clinician at the site of data collection, or a clinician external to the study where the diagnostic assessment predated collection. No further annotator demographic information is recorded.
Human-level performance on the applications the dataset is intended to address is described as varying widely.

Whisper Large generated transcriptions; openSMILE extracted acoustic features capturing temporal dynamics; Praat through the Parselmouth interface produced phonetic and prosodic measures of fundamental frequency, formants and voice quality; torchaudio produced spectrograms, Mel spectrograms, MFCCs and pitch contours; sparc produced electromagnetic articulography estimates together with loudness, periodicity and pitch; ppgs produced high-fidelity neural phonetic posteriorgrams. b2aiprep organized and preprocessed the dataset and SenseLab processed the audio files; this release was generated with b2aiprep version 3.0.0.
Certain aspects of the data, for example transcription, were generated using off-the-shelf models that have not been audited for correctness.

Derived audio features for the retained recordings. Dense per-frame features are distributed as Apache Parquet, an open-source column-oriented data file format, each element carrying participant_id, session_id, task_name, n_frames and the feature tensor. Recording-level summaries are distributed as tab-delimited text. Every data file is accompanied by a JSON data dictionary sharing its file stem, describing the feature and the processing applied.
Spectrograms of dimension 201 by T for 29,278 recordings, generated with a 25 ms window size, 10 ms hop length and a 400-point FFT.
Mel spectrograms of dimension 60 by T for 29,278 recordings, generated with a 25 ms window size, 10 ms hop length, a 400-point FFT and 60 Mel bins.
Mel-frequency cepstrum coefficients of dimension 60 by T for 29,278 recordings, using the same parameters as the Mel spectrograms.
Detected pitch, the fundamental frequency, over time, of dimension T for 32,522 recordings, with a minimum and maximum pitch of 80 and 500 Hz.

Estimated electromagnetic articulography for 28,640 recordings, of dimension T by 12, the twelve channels being X and Y positions of six articulators: tongue dorsum, tongue body, tongue tip, lower incisor, upper lip and lower lip.
Estimated loudness for 31,855 recordings, based on the average absolute amplitude of the audio waveform in 20 ms windows, of dimension T.
Estimated periodicity, the confidence of pitch presence, for 31,872 recordings, derived using 20 ms windows, of dimension T.
Estimated fundamental frequency for 31,872 recordings, computed with a different algorithm from the torchaudio pitch, over a range of 50 to 550 Hz, of dimension T.
Phonetic posteriorgram probabilities across 40 phoneme categories for 29,289 recordings, of dimension 40 by T at a frame rate of 100 Hz.
Recording-level features derived from the raw audio using openSMILE, Praat, Parselmouth and torchaudio, one row per unique recording and one column per feature.
Quality control metrics derived from the raw audio, one feature per audio recording. Introduced in version 3.1.0.

A binary Parquet file and its corresponding data dictionary carrying per-recording metadata, including task instructions and prompts and information about the microphone used and its gain. Introduced in version 3.1.0.

Tab-delimited tables of information collected from the participant or another informant during the encounter, organized into confounders, demographics, diagnosis, enrollment, questionnaire and task subfolders. The diagnosis subfolder holds one table per condition, covering airway stenosis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, anxiety, benign lesions, bipolar disorder, cognitive impairment, control, COPD and asthma, depression, glottic insufficiency, laryngeal cancer, laryngeal dystonia, laryngitis, muscle tension dysphonia, Parkinson's disease, precancerous lesions, unexplained chronic cough and unilateral vocal fold paralysis. The questionnaire subfolder holds the ADHD adult, custom affect scale, DSM-5 adult, dyspnea index, GAD-7, Leicester cough questionnaire, PANAS, PHQ-9, productive vocabulary, psychiatric history, PTSD adult, VHI-10 and voice perception instruments. The task subfolder holds acoustic task, Harvard sentences, random item generation, recording, session, Stroop and Winograd tables. Every table is paired with a JSON data dictionary whose keys match the table's column names and whose values give a one-sentence description, the question asked of the participant where applicable, and the data type of the response.

Referent: this record describes the adult Bridge2AI-Voice dataset at version 3.1.0 as published on PhysioNet, the highest-ranked non-superseded source in the declared bundle. The pediatric cohort is a separate PhysioNet release and is recorded under related_datasets rather than as part of this dataset. Statements drawn from the project documentation and the IRB protocol that describe planned or future collection, other versions, or the pediatric cohort are marked as such where used. Target size: the project documentation states an anticipated enrollment of 10,000 by 2027 and describes a flagship dataset of 10,000 voices, while the IRB protocol, at the same source rank, states a sample size of 30,000 participants, and the audiomics white paper states a primary deliverable of a publicly available database of 30,000 human voices. The two tier-2 sources cannot be separated by rank, so neither figure is recorded as dataset content; both are goals rather than realized collection, against 833 participants actually released. The consortium publishes an AI-readiness self-assessment against the Bridge2AI recommendations, scoring 100 per cent on FAIRness, provenance, pre-model explainability and ethics, 80 per cent on characterization (data quality criterion unmet), 75 per cent on computability (contextualization criterion unmet) and 50 per cent on sustainability (domain-appropriate and associated criteria unmet).

values.text: Bridge2AI-Voice: An ethically-sourced, diverse voice dataset linked to health information

Bridge2AI-Voice is an ethically sourced, multi-site dataset of voice, speech, breathing and cough data linked to demographic, clinical and validated-questionnaire information, built to support research into voice as a biomarker of health. Version 3.1.0 covers 833 adult participants recruited at five North American sites and selected for conditions that manifest within the voice waveform: voice disorders, neurological and neurodegenerative disorders, mood and psychiatric disorders and respiratory disorders, alongside control participants. Participants completed a standardized protocol of acoustic tasks on a tablet application, with a headset where possible, together with demographic, confounder, disease-specific and validated-questionnaire instruments; clinical diagnoses were validated by clinicians against site gold standards. The public release distributes data considered low risk — spectrograms, Mel spectrograms, MFCCs, pitch and periodicity traces, Speech Articulatory Coding articulatory estimates, phonetic posteriorgrams, openSMILE, Praat and parselmouth static features, per-recording audio quality metrics, per-recording metadata and phenotype tables — rather than the original waveforms. Raw audio is disseminated separately, under controlled access only.

Raw audio recordings of standardized acoustic tasks captured by the Bridge2AI-Voice tablet application, together with questionnaire and clinical data captured in REDCap, collected under the Bridge2AI Voice Data Acquisition protocol.

Bensoussan, Y., Sigaras, A., Rameau, A., Elemento, O., Powell, M., Dorr, D., Payne, P., Ravitsky, V., Bélisle-Pipon, J., Bahr, R., Watts, S., Bolser, D., Siu, J., Lerner-Ellis, J., Rudzicz, F., Boyer, M., Abdel-Aty, Y., Ahmed Syed, T., Anibal, J., ... Ghosh, S. (2026). Bridge2AI-Voice: An ethically-sourced, diverse voice dataset linked to health information (version 3.1.0). PhysioNet. RRID:SCR_007345. https://doi.org/10.13026/8xbn-nq66

This record describes the adult Bridge2AI-Voice dataset at PhysioNet version 3.1.0, published 2026-05-01, which is the most recent version present in the source bundle; the Bridge2AI-Voice Pediatric Dataset is recorded as a related dataset rather than as part of this one. The project documentation at docs.b2ai-voice.org answers several healthsheet questions against earlier releases — it reports "version 3.0 containing ~61,937 voice-derived recordings from 833 adult participants", heads its de-identification section "Methods of De-identification for v3.0.0", and elsewhere refers to "The current v.2.0.0 dataset"; where that documentation and the PhysioNet 3.1.0 record differ, the higher-ranked PhysioNet record has been preferred here. The documentation also gives distribution and maintenance answers for the Health Data Nexus platform, where version 1.0 was published, while versions 1.1 onward are published on PhysioNet. Email addresses in the scraped documentation are redacted as "[email protected]", so only the DACO@b2ai-voice.org address that appears verbatim in the PhysioNet notices is recorded. The award identifier is written variously across sources: the PhysioNet acknowledgement gives "3OT2OD032720-01S1", NIH RePORTER gives application "3OT2OD032720-01S3" under core project "OT2OD032720", and the documentation footer gives "Award #3Tf-OTOD03272001S2" and "3TF-OT2ActfOD032720Projectf01S1", both apparently corrupted in transcription. The 2025 feasibility publication in the bundle reports a separate 47-participant study of the collection application under USF IRB 004890 and its participant characteristics, task metrics and limitations are not attributed to this dataset.
To create an ethically sourced flagship dataset that enables future research in artificial intelligence and supports critical insights into the use of voice as a biomarker of health.

To generate a large multi-institutional, ethically sourced and diverse voice dataset linked to multimodal health biomarkers in order to fuel voice AI research and promote integration of voice as a biomarker of health in clinical care.

To enable the development, benchmarking or validation of clinically applicable machine-learning models for diagnosing a wide range of health conditions using voice data, including vocal pathologies and neurological, psychiatric, respiratory and pediatric voice disorders.

The absence of large-scale, diverse and well-documented voice data for clinical machine-learning applications. Previous studies of machine learning-based voice diagnosis produced promising results, but their sample sizes were too small or they lacked the key metadata needed for training robust, clinically useful models.
The absence of standards for how voice and speech data are collected, which makes comparing studies and pooling data across them difficult.
The confinement of existing work to small- to medium-sized datasets with limited data outside acoustic measures and no linkage to multi-modal health data.

Training machine-learning models for disease detection and classification using voice data, with labels drawn from diagnostic categories including vocal pathologies, neurological disorders, psychiatric conditions and respiratory disorders.
Screening, diagnosis and monitoring of health conditions through voice biomarkers.
Cohort selection: the questionnaire-derived phenotype tables distributed in the phenotype folder can be used to select cohorts for downstream analysis.

The dataset is primarily intended for research applications, specifically the development of AI and machine-learning models for healthcare, and it supports clinical research in disease screening, diagnosis and monitoring through voice biomarkers.
Under the Registered Access Agreement the dataset is intended solely for commercial and non-commercial research purposes by Authorized Researchers.

Non-clinical and non-research applications such as hiring decisions, insurance premium adjustments, or any form of surveillance that could lead to discrimination or harm. These limitations are intended to prevent unethical or biased outcomes that could negatively impact individuals based on their health conditions or voice characteristics.
Attempting to re-identify research participants, or taking any action that could reasonably lead to re-identification, is not permitted under the Registered Data Access Agreement.
Any purpose that could foreseeably cause harm or stigmatization to research participants, their families, communities or specific populations is not permitted.

Intellectual property protections, database rights or related rights may not be used in a manner that restricts or limits access to any part of the dataset or to any conclusions derived from it, so that future use of the dataset remains unrestricted in alignment with Open Science principles.
Co-principal investigator of the Bridge2AI-Voice project and co-lead of the data acquisition module; first author of the version 3.1.0 release.
